chandogya-3-5-4.translation: These are the essence of essences, for the Vedas are essences and these are their essences. These are the nectar of nectars, for the Vedas are nectar and these are their nectar.
chandogya-3-5-4.meaning: The sun's colours are the very best of the Vedas.
chandogya-3-5-4.explanation: The section sums up: the colours of the sun are the distilled essence of all sacred knowledge.

chandogya-3-6-1.translation: The first nectar is what the Vasus live on, with Agni (fire) as their mouth. The gods do not eat or drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this nectar.
chandogya-3-6-1.meaning: The Vasus are fed simply by seeing the sun's first nectar.
chandogya-3-6-1.explanation: Gods do not need food; contemplating the nectar is enough. This is a picture of joy through vision rather than consumption.

chandogya-3-6-2.translation: They enter into that form and rise up out of that form.
chandogya-3-6-2.meaning: The gods rest in this colour of the sun and rise from it again.
chandogya-3-6-2.explanation: The gods go in and out of the sun's colours as it rises and sets.

chandogya-3-6-3.translation: Whoever knows this nectar becomes one of the Vasus, and with Agni (fire) as mouth, seeing this nectar, is satisfied. He enters that form and rises out of it.
chandogya-3-6-3.meaning: The one who knows this joins the Vasus and shares their joy.
chandogya-3-6-3.explanation: Knowledge brings the knower into the company of the gods.

chandogya-3-6-4.translation: As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so long will he enjoy the rule and self-rule of the Vasus.
chandogya-3-6-4.meaning: The knower shares the rule of the Vasus for a vast age.
chandogya-3-6-4.explanation: The text imagines immense cosmic ages, each twice as long as the last, in which the sun moves in different directions.

chandogya-3-7-1.translation: The second nectar is what the Rudras live on, with Indra as their mouth. The gods do not eat or drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this nectar.
chandogya-3-7-1.meaning: The Rudras are fed simply by seeing the sun's second nectar.

chandogya-3-7-2.meaning: The gods rest in this colour of the sun and rise from it again.
chandogya-3-7-2.explanation: The gods go in and out of the sun's colours as it rises and sets.

chandogya-3-7-3.translation: Whoever knows this nectar becomes one of the Rudras, and with Indra as mouth, seeing this nectar, is satisfied. He enters that form and rises out of it.
chandogya-3-7-3.meaning: The one who knows this joins the Rudras and shares their joy.
chandogya-3-7-3.explanation: Knowledge brings the knower into the company of the gods.

chandogya-3-7-4.translation: Twice as long as that, the sun rises in the south and sets in the north; for so long will he enjoy the rule and self-rule of the Rudras.
chandogya-3-7-4.meaning: The knower shares the rule of the Rudras for a vast age.
chandogya-3-7-4.explanation: The text imagines immense cosmic ages, each twice as long as the last, in which the sun moves in different directions.

chandogya-3-8-1.meaning: The Adityas are fed simply by seeing the sun's third nectar.
chandogya-3-8-1.explanation: Gods do not need food; contemplating the nectar is enough. This is a picture of joy through vision rather than consumption.

chandogya-3-8-2.meaning: The gods rest in this colour of the sun and rise from it again.
chandogya-3-8-2.explanation: The gods go in and out of the sun's colours as it rises and sets.

chandogya-3-8-3.translation: Whoever knows this nectar becomes one of the Adityas, and with Varuna as mouth, seeing this nectar, is satisfied. He enters that form and rises out of it.
chandogya-3-8-3.meaning: The one who knows this joins the Adityas and shares their joy.
chandogya-3-8-3.explanation: Knowledge brings the knower into the company of the gods.

chandogya-3-8-4.translation: Twice as long as that, the sun rises in the west and sets in the east; for so long will he enjoy the rule and self-rule of the Adityas.
chandogya-3-8-4.meaning: The knower shares the rule of the Adityas for a vast age.
chandogya-3-8-4.explanation: The text imagines immense cosmic ages, each twice as long as the last, in which the sun moves in different directions.

chandogya-3-9-1.translation: The fourth nectar is what the Maruts live on, with Soma as their mouth. The gods do not eat or drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this nectar.
chandogya-3-9-1.meaning: The Maruts are fed simply by seeing the sun's fourth nectar.
chandogya-3-9-1.explanation: Gods do not need food; contemplating the nectar is enough. This is a picture of joy through vision rather than consumption.

chandogya-3-9-2.translation: They enter into that form and rise up out of that form.
chandogya-3-9-2.meaning: The gods rest in this colour of the sun and rise from it again.
chandogya-3-9-2.explanation: The gods go in and out of the sun's colours as it rises and sets.

chandogya-3-9-3.translation: Whoever knows this nectar becomes one of the Maruts, and with Soma as mouth, seeing this nectar, is satisfied. He enters that form and rises out of it.
chandogya-3-9-3.meaning: The one who knows this joins the Maruts and shares their joy.
chandogya-3-9-3.explanation: Knowledge brings the knower into the company of the gods.

chandogya-3-9-4.translation: Twice as long as that, the sun rises in the north and sets in the south; for so long will he enjoy the rule and self-rule of the Maruts.
chandogya-3-9-4.meaning: The knower shares the rule of the Maruts for a vast age.
chandogya-3-9-4.explanation: The text imagines immense cosmic ages, each twice as long as the last, in which the sun moves in different directions.

chandogya-3-10-1.translation: The fifth nectar is what the Sadhyas live on, with Brahman as their mouth. The gods do not eat or drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this nectar.
chandogya-3-10-1.meaning: The Sadhyas are fed simply by seeing the sun's fifth nectar.
chandogya-3-10-1.explanation: Gods do not need food; contemplating the nectar is enough. This is a picture of joy through vision rather than consumption.

chandogya-3-10-2.translation: They enter into that form and rise up out of that form.
chandogya-3-10-2.meaning: The gods rest in this colour of the sun and rise from it again.
chandogya-3-10-2.explanation: The gods go in and out of the sun's colours as it rises and sets.

chandogya-3-10-3.translation: Whoever knows this nectar becomes one of the Sadhyas, and with Brahman as mouth, seeing this nectar, is satisfied. He enters that form and rises out of it.
chandogya-3-10-3.meaning: The one who knows this joins the Sadhyas and shares their joy.
chandogya-3-10-3.explanation: Knowledge brings the knower into the company of the gods.

chandogya-3-10-4.translation: Twice as long as that, the sun rises in the zenith and sets below; for so long will he enjoy the rule and self-rule of the Sadhyas.
chandogya-3-10-4.meaning: The knower shares the rule of the Sadhyas for a vast age.
chandogya-3-10-4.explanation: The text imagines immense cosmic ages, each twice as long as the last, in which the sun moves in different directions.

chandogya-3-11-1.translation: After that, having risen to the zenith, it will neither rise nor set; it will stand alone in the middle. There is this verse:
chandogya-3-11-1.meaning: In the end the sun stands still, neither rising nor setting.
chandogya-3-11-1.explanation: Beyond all the ages, there is a state where time stops. This points to Brahman, which is beyond change.

chandogya-3-11-2.translation: 'There it never sets, and never has it risen. O gods, by this truth, may I not lose Brahman.'
chandogya-3-11-2.meaning: In that state there is no sunrise or sunset; may I never lose it.
chandogya-3-11-2.explanation: A prayer by one who has seen the timeless light.

chandogya-3-11-3.translation: For one who knows this secret teaching of Brahman, the sun neither rises nor sets; for him it is always day.
chandogya-3-11-3.meaning: For the one who knows Brahman, it is always day.
chandogya-3-11-3.explanation: A beautiful image of enlightenment: a light that never sets.

chandogya-3-11-4.translation: Brahma taught this to Prajapati, Prajapati to Manu, Manu to his descendants. And the father taught this Brahman to Uddalaka Aruni, his eldest son.
chandogya-3-11-4.meaning: This teaching was passed from the creator down through generations.
chandogya-3-11-4.explanation: A line of teachers shows the teaching's sacred origin.

chandogya-3-11-5.translation: A father should teach this Brahman only to his eldest son or to a worthy pupil,
chandogya-3-11-5.meaning: This teaching should be given only to a worthy student.
chandogya-3-11-5.explanation: The teaching is guarded and given with care.

chandogya-3-11-6.translation: and to no one else, even if one were to give him this whole earth surrounded by water and full of riches. For this is worth more than that.
chandogya-3-11-6.meaning: This knowledge is worth more than the whole world's wealth.

chandogya-3-12-1.translation: The Gayatri is all this, whatever exists. Speech is the Gayatri, for speech sings and protects all that exists.
chandogya-3-12-1.meaning: The Gayatri verse is everything; speech sings and protects all beings.
chandogya-3-12-1.explanation: Gayatri is the most famous Vedic metre and prayer. Its name is explained as gayati (sings) and trayate (protects).

chandogya-3-12-2.translation: That Gayatri is this earth, for everything that exists rests on it and does not go beyond it.
chandogya-3-12-2.meaning: The Gayatri is like the earth: all beings stand on it.
chandogya-3-12-2.explanation: The Gayatri is now identified with the earth, the support of all.

chandogya-3-12-3.translation: That earth is the body of a person, for the life-breaths rest in it and do not go beyond it.
chandogya-3-12-3.meaning: The body is the earth of a person; life rests in it.
chandogya-3-12-3.explanation: The same pattern moves from the world into the human being.

chandogya-3-12-4.translation: That body is the heart within the person, for the life-breaths rest in it and do not go beyond it.
chandogya-3-12-4.meaning: At the deepest level, life rests in the heart.
chandogya-3-12-4.explanation: The search moves further inward, to the heart.

chandogya-3-12-5.translation: This Gayatri has four feet and six forms. A Rig verse says this:
chandogya-3-12-5.meaning: The Gayatri has four parts and six forms.
chandogya-3-12-5.explanation: The six are being, speech, earth, body, heart and breaths; a Rig Veda verse follows.

chandogya-3-12-6.translation: 'Such is its greatness, yet the Person is greater still. All beings are one quarter of him; three quarters, immortal, are in heaven.'
chandogya-3-12-6.meaning: All the world is only a quarter of the divine; the rest is beyond.
chandogya-3-12-6.explanation: A quotation from the Purusha Sukta (Rig Veda 10.90): the visible universe is a small part of the infinite.

chandogya-3-12-7.translation: What is called Brahman is the space outside a person. And the space outside a person
chandogya-3-12-7.meaning: Brahman is the space all around us,
chandogya-3-12-7.explanation: The teaching moves from outer space to inner space.

chandogya-3-12-8.translation: is the space inside a person. And the space inside a person
chandogya-3-12-8.meaning: which is the same as the space within us,
chandogya-3-12-8.explanation: The space outside and inside are one.

chandogya-3-12-9.translation: is the space within the heart. That is full and unchanging. Whoever knows this gains full and unchanging good fortune.
chandogya-3-12-9.meaning: which is the space in the heart: full and never-changing.
chandogya-3-12-9.explanation: The 'space in the heart' is a key Upanishadic image for Brahman found within.

chandogya-3-13-1.translation: The heart has five openings for the gods. Its eastern opening is the in-breath, the eye, the sun. One should worship it as brilliance and food. Whoever knows this becomes brilliant and enjoys food.
chandogya-3-13-1.meaning: The heart has five doors; the eastern one is breath, sight and the sun.
chandogya-3-13-1.explanation: Each opening of the heart is linked to a life-breath, a sense and a god.

chandogya-3-13-2.translation: Its southern opening is the diffused breath, the ear, the moon. One should worship it as prosperity and fame. Whoever knows this becomes prosperous and famous.
chandogya-3-13-2.meaning: The southern door is the spreading breath, hearing and the moon.
chandogya-3-13-2.explanation: Vyana is the breath that spreads through the body.

chandogya-3-13-3.translation: Its western opening is the out-breath, speech, fire. One should worship it as sacred radiance and food. Whoever knows this becomes radiant and enjoys food.
chandogya-3-13-3.meaning: The western door is the out-breath, speech and fire.
chandogya-3-13-3.explanation: Apana is the downward or outward breath.

chandogya-3-13-4.translation: Its northern opening is the balancing breath, the mind, the rain-god. One should worship it as fame and beauty. Whoever knows this becomes famous and beautiful.
chandogya-3-13-4.meaning: The northern door is the balancing breath, the mind and rain.
chandogya-3-13-4.explanation: Samana is the breath that balances and digests.

chandogya-3-13-5.translation: Its upper opening is the upward breath, wind, space. One should worship it as strength and greatness. Whoever knows this becomes strong and great.
chandogya-3-13-5.meaning: The upper door is the rising breath, wind and space.
chandogya-3-13-5.explanation: Udana is the upward breath, thought to carry the self out at death.

chandogya-3-13-6.translation: These are the five servants of Brahman, the door-keepers of heaven. Whoever knows them so has a hero born in his family and reaches heaven.
chandogya-3-13-6.meaning: These five are the gatekeepers of heaven.
chandogya-3-13-6.explanation: The breaths guard the way to the divine within the heart.

chandogya-3-13-7.translation: The light that shines above this heaven, above all, in the highest worlds beyond which there are none, is the same as the light within a person. We see it when we feel warmth by touching the body; we hear it when we cover our ears and hear a sound like a roar or a blazing fire. One should worship it as seen and heard. Whoever knows this becomes beautiful and renowned.
chandogya-3-13-7.meaning: The light beyond the highest heaven is the same light that lives inside you.
chandogya-3-13-7.explanation: A famous verse: the cosmic light is the inner light, felt as the body's warmth and heard as the inner hum when the ears are covered.

chandogya-3-14-1.translation: All this is Brahman. From it all things arise, in it they live, into it they dissolve; so one should meditate on it calmly. A person is made of intention. As one's intention is in this world, so one becomes after leaving it. So one should form a good intention.
chandogya-3-14-1.meaning: Everything is Brahman, and we become what we deeply intend.
chandogya-3-14-1.explanation: Shandilya's famous teaching begins. Tajjalan is a compressed word: born from it (ja), dissolving into it (la), living in it (an).

chandogya-3-14-2.translation: He is made of mind, his body is life, his form is light, his will is truth, his self is space. He contains all actions, all desires, all smells, all tastes; he holds all this, without speech, without care.
chandogya-3-14-2.meaning: The inner Self is mind, life, light and truth, and holds everything.
chandogya-3-14-2.explanation: A description of the Self (atman) as both personal and universal.

chandogya-3-14-3.translation: This self of mine within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice, or barley, or a mustard seed, or a millet grain or its kernel. This self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth, greater than the sky, greater than heaven, greater than all these worlds.
chandogya-3-14-3.meaning: The Self in your heart is tinier than a seed and bigger than all the worlds.
chandogya-3-14-3.explanation: One of the best-loved verses of the Upanishads: the Self is both infinitely small and infinitely great.

chandogya-3-14-4.translation: Containing all actions, all desires, all smells, all tastes, holding all this, without speech, without care: this is my self within the heart. This is Brahman. When I leave this world I shall become one with it. One who believes this has no doubt. So said Shandilya.
chandogya-3-14-4.meaning: The Self in the heart is Brahman, and at death I will merge with it.
chandogya-3-14-4.explanation: Shandilya's teaching ends with complete confidence: the inner Self and the infinite are one.

chandogya-3-15-1.translation: The chest whose inside is the sky and whose bottom is the earth does not decay. The directions are its corners, heaven its upper lid. This chest holds all treasures; the whole universe rests in it.
chandogya-3-15-1.meaning: The universe is like a chest that never decays and holds all treasures.
chandogya-3-15-1.explanation: The cosmos is pictured as a treasure box.

chandogya-3-15-2.translation: Its eastern quarter is called Juhu, the southern Sahamana, the western Rajni, the northern Subhuta. The wind is their child. Whoever knows the wind as the child of the directions never weeps for a son. I know the wind as the child of the directions; may I not weep for a son.
chandogya-3-15-2.meaning: Knowing the wind as the child of the directions protects one from grieving for a child.
chandogya-3-15-2.explanation: A father's prayer for his son's long life, using the wind, which never dies, as a symbol.

chandogya-3-15-3.translation: I take refuge in the imperishable chest, for this one, this one, this one. I take refuge in breath, for this one... I take refuge in bhur, in bhuvah, in svah, for this one, this one, this one.
chandogya-3-15-3.meaning: The father seeks protection for his son in the universe, in breath and in the three worlds.
chandogya-3-15-3.explanation: 'This one' stands for the son's name, said three times. The prayer seeks shelter for the child in everything.

chandogya-3-15-4.translation: When I said, 'I take refuge in breath,' breath is all that exists, whatever there is. So I took refuge in all of that.
chandogya-3-15-4.meaning: Breath stands for all life, so taking refuge in it is taking refuge in everything.
chandogya-3-15-4.explanation: The father explains each part of his prayer.

chandogya-3-15-6.translation: When I said, 'I take refuge in bhuvah,' I meant: I take refuge in fire, in wind, in the sun.
chandogya-3-15-6.meaning: The second sacred word means fire, wind and sun.
chandogya-3-15-6.explanation: Each sacred word stands for three powers. (Verse 3.15.5 is missing in the digital source.)

chandogya-3-15-7.translation: When I said, 'I take refuge in svah,' I meant: I take refuge in the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Sama Veda.
chandogya-3-15-7.meaning: The third sacred word means the three Vedas.
chandogya-3-15-7.explanation: The prayer closes by taking refuge in sacred knowledge.

chandogya-3-16-1.translation: The person is the sacrifice. His first twenty-four years are the morning pressing, for the Gayatri has twenty-four syllables and that pressing belongs to the Gayatri. The Vasus are linked to it. The life-breaths are the Vasus, for they make all this dwell (vasayanti).
chandogya-3-16-1.meaning: A human life is like a sacrifice; this stage of life belongs to the Vasus.
chandogya-3-16-1.explanation: A whole life is pictured as a day-long Soma rite. Each stage matches a pressing, a metre and a group of gods. The first 24 years are youth.

chandogya-3-16-2.translation: If anything troubles him at this age, he should say: 'Life-breaths, Vasus, extend my morning pressing into the midday. Let me, the sacrifice, not be lost among the life-breaths, the Vasus.' He rises from that illness and becomes well.
chandogya-3-16-2.meaning: In illness, one can pray for life to continue to its next stage.
chandogya-3-16-2.explanation: A prayer for health, framed in the language of the sacrifice.

chandogya-3-16-3.translation: The person is the sacrifice. His first forty-four years are the midday pressing, for the Trishtubh has forty-four syllables and that pressing belongs to the Trishtubh. The Rudras are linked to it. The life-breaths are the Rudras, for they make all this weep (rodayanti).
chandogya-3-16-3.meaning: A human life is like a sacrifice; this stage of life belongs to the Rudras.
chandogya-3-16-3.explanation: A whole life is pictured as a day-long Soma rite. Each stage matches a pressing, a metre and a group of gods. The next 44 years are the middle of life.

chandogya-3-16-4.translation: If anything troubles him at this age, he should say: 'Life-breaths, Rudras, extend my midday pressing into the third. Let me, the sacrifice, not be lost among the life-breaths, the Rudras.' He rises from that illness and becomes well.
chandogya-3-16-4.meaning: In illness, one can pray for life to continue to its next stage.
chandogya-3-16-4.explanation: A prayer for health, framed in the language of the sacrifice.

chandogya-3-16-5.translation: The person is the sacrifice. His first forty-eight years are the third pressing, for the Jagati has forty-eight syllables and that pressing belongs to the Jagati. The Adityas are linked to it. The life-breaths are the Adityas, for they take all this to themselves (adadate).
chandogya-3-16-5.meaning: A human life is like a sacrifice; this stage of life belongs to the Adityas.
chandogya-3-16-5.explanation: A whole life is pictured as a day-long Soma rite. Each stage matches a pressing, a metre and a group of gods. The last 48 years complete a full life of 116 years.

chandogya-3-16-6.translation: If anything troubles him at this age, he should say: 'Life-breaths, Adityas, extend my third pressing to a full life. Let me, the sacrifice, not be lost among the life-breaths, the Adityas.' He rises from that illness and becomes well.
chandogya-3-16-6.meaning: In old age too one can pray for life to reach its full length.
chandogya-3-16-6.explanation: The prayer for the final stage of life.

chandogya-3-16-7.translation: Knowing this, Mahidasa Aitareya said: 'Why do you trouble me, illness, when I will not die of you?' He lived a hundred and sixteen years. Whoever knows this lives a hundred and sixteen years.
chandogya-3-16-7.meaning: A sage who knew this lived 116 years.
chandogya-3-16-7.explanation: Mahidasa Aitareya, the sage of the Aitareya texts, spoke boldly to his illness. 24 + 44 + 48 = 116.

chandogya-3-17-1.translation: When a person feels hunger, thirst and has no pleasure, that is his consecration.
chandogya-3-17-1.meaning: Hardship in life is like the first step of a sacrifice.
chandogya-3-17-1.explanation: A whole life is again compared to the Soma rite. The difficult times are the diksha, the consecration with its fasting.

chandogya-3-17-2.translation: When he eats, drinks and enjoys himself, that is like the upasad ceremonies.
chandogya-3-17-2.meaning: Eating and enjoyment are part of the sacred rite too.
chandogya-3-17-2.explanation: The upasad days of the ritual allowed some food.

chandogya-3-17-3.translation: When he laughs, feasts and makes love, that is like the hymns and recitations.
chandogya-3-17-3.meaning: Laughter and love are like the chants of the sacrifice.
chandogya-3-17-3.explanation: Every part of life is sacred in this view.

chandogya-3-17-4.translation: Austerity, generosity, honesty, non-violence and truthfulness: these are his gifts to the priests.
chandogya-3-17-4.meaning: Discipline, giving, honesty, non-harming and truth are the true offerings.
chandogya-3-17-4.explanation: A key ethical verse: the real fees of life's sacrifice are virtues.

chandogya-3-17-5.translation: So people say 'He will press' and 'He has pressed', meaning 'he will be born' and 'he was born'. That is his rebirth. Death is the final bath.
chandogya-3-17-5.meaning: Birth is the pressing of the Soma, and death is the closing bath.
chandogya-3-17-5.explanation: Word-play on su (press) and su (give birth). The avabhritha is the ritual bath at the end of a sacrifice.

chandogya-3-17-6.translation: Ghora Angirasa taught this to Krishna, son of Devaki, and said he became free from thirst. At the time of death one should take refuge in these three: 'You are the imperishable; you are the unshakable; you are the very essence of life.' There are two Rig verses on this:
chandogya-3-17-6.meaning: A sage taught Krishna son of Devaki what to remember at death.
chandogya-3-17-6.explanation: This is the earliest mention of a Krishna son of Devaki in Sanskrit literature. Whether he is the Krishna of the Gita is debated.

chandogya-3-17-7.translation: 'They see the morning light of the ancient seed, shining above the darkness.' 'Seeing the higher light, seeing the higher heaven, we have reached the sun, god among the gods, the highest light, the highest light.'
chandogya-3-17-7.meaning: Rising above darkness, we reach the highest light.
chandogya-3-17-7.explanation: Two Rig Veda verses about seeing the light beyond darkness close the section.

chandogya-3-18-1.translation: One should meditate on the mind as Brahman; that is about the self. Now about the gods: space is Brahman. So both are taught, the inner and the outer.
chandogya-3-18-1.meaning: Mind within and space without can both be seen as Brahman.
chandogya-3-18-1.explanation: A paired meditation: one inward, one outward.

chandogya-3-18-2.translation: This Brahman has four feet. Speech is one foot, breath one, the eye one, the ear one: that is the inner. Fire is one foot, wind one, the sun one, the directions one: that is the outer.
chandogya-3-18-2.meaning: Brahman has four parts within us and four in the world.
chandogya-3-18-2.explanation: Each sense matches a cosmic power.

chandogya-3-18-3.translation: Speech is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with the light of fire. Whoever knows this shines and glows with fame, renown and sacred radiance.
chandogya-3-18-3.explanation: Speech is lit by fire as its outer partner.

chandogya-3-18-4.translation: Breath is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with the light of wind. Whoever knows this shines and glows with fame, renown and sacred radiance.
chandogya-3-18-4.meaning: Breath shines with the wind's light.

chandogya-3-18-5.translation: The eye is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with the light of the sun. Whoever knows this shines and glows with fame, renown and sacred radiance.
chandogya-3-18-5.meaning: The eye shines with the sun's light.
chandogya-3-18-5.explanation: Sight is paired with the sun.

chandogya-3-18-6.translation: The ear is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with the light of the directions. Whoever knows this shines and glows with fame, renown and sacred radiance.
chandogya-3-18-6.meaning: The ear shines with the light of the directions.
chandogya-3-18-6.explanation: Hearing is paired with the directions, from which sound comes.

chandogya-3-19-1.translation: The teaching is: the sun is Brahman. Its explanation: in the beginning this was non-being. It became being. It grew and turned into an egg. It lay for a year, then split open. The two halves of the shell became silver and gold.
chandogya-3-19-1.meaning: Creation began as a cosmic egg that split into silver and gold.
chandogya-3-19-1.explanation: A creation story: the world egg, a common image in Indian thought.

chandogya-3-19-2.translation: The silver half is this earth; the gold half is heaven. The thick membrane became the mountains; the thin membrane the clouds and mist; the veins the rivers; the fluid inside the ocean.
chandogya-3-19-2.meaning: Every part of the egg became part of the world.
chandogya-3-19-2.explanation: The parts of an egg are matched to the features of the landscape.

chandogya-3-19-3.translation: What was born from it is the sun. When it was born, shouts of joy rose up, and all beings and all desires. So at its every rising and return, shouts of joy rise up, and all beings and all desires.
chandogya-3-19-3.meaning: The sun was born from the egg, and all life rejoices at its rising.
chandogya-3-19-3.explanation: Each sunrise repeats the joy of creation.

chandogya-3-19-4.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on the sun as Brahman, pleasant sounds will quickly come to him and delight him.
chandogya-3-19-4.meaning: Seeing the sun as Brahman brings joy into life.

chandogya-4-1-1.translation: There was once Janashruti Pautrayana, a faithful and generous giver who served much food. He had rest-houses built everywhere, thinking, 'People everywhere will eat my food.'
chandogya-4-1-1.meaning: A generous king feeds people everywhere.
chandogya-4-1-1.explanation: Chapter 4 opens with the story of King Janashruti and the humble sage Raikva.

chandogya-4-1-2.translation: One night some geese flew over. One goose said to another, 'Hey, Bhallaksha! The light of Janashruti Pautrayana spreads like the sky. Don't touch it or it will burn you.'
chandogya-4-1-2.meaning: Passing geese praise the king's glory.
chandogya-4-1-2.explanation: Talking birds act as messengers in this story.

chandogya-4-1-3.translation: The other replied, 'Who is he, that you speak of him as if he were Raikva with the cart?' 'What is Raikva with the cart like?'
chandogya-4-1-3.meaning: The second goose says the king is nothing compared to Raikva.
chandogya-4-1-3.explanation: Raikva is a sage who lives under a cart.

chandogya-4-1-4.translation: 'As all the lower throws go to the one who wins with the highest throw of the dice, so all the good that people do goes to him. And whoever knows what he knows, I say the same of him.'
chandogya-4-1-4.meaning: All the good people do flows to the wise Raikva.
chandogya-4-1-4.explanation: The image is from dice: the top throw collects all the lower ones. Knowledge outranks generosity.

chandogya-4-1-5.translation: Janashruti Pautrayana overheard this. As soon as he got up, he said to his attendant, 'You speak of me as if I were Raikva with the cart!' 'What is Raikva with the cart like?'
chandogya-4-1-5.meaning: The king overhears and wants to find Raikva.
chandogya-4-1-5.explanation: The king is humbled and curious.

chandogya-4-1-6.translation: 'As all the lower throws go to the one who wins with the highest throw, so all the good that people do goes to him. And whoever knows what he knows, I say the same of him.'
chandogya-4-1-6.meaning: The king repeats what the goose said.
chandogya-4-1-6.explanation: The king tells his attendant what he heard.

chandogya-4-1-7.translation: The attendant searched and came back saying, 'I did not find him.' The king said, 'Look for him where one would look for a brahmin.'
chandogya-4-1-7.meaning: The king tells his servant to look in the right places.
chandogya-4-1-7.explanation: The servant looked in towns; the king tells him to look in lonely places where sages live.

chandogya-4-1-8.translation: He found a man under a cart, scratching his itching skin, and sat down beside him. 'Sir, are you Raikva with the cart?' 'Yes, I am,' he replied. The attendant returned, saying, 'I have found him.'
chandogya-4-1-8.meaning: Raikva is found living poorly under a cart.
chandogya-4-1-8.explanation: The wise man lives in poverty, caring nothing for comfort.

chandogya-4-2-1.translation: Janashruti Pautrayana took six hundred cows, a gold necklace and a chariot drawn by mules, and went to him. He said,
chandogya-4-2-1.meaning: The king brings rich gifts to Raikva.
chandogya-4-2-1.explanation: The king hopes to buy the teaching.

chandogya-4-2-2.translation: 'Raikva, here are six hundred cows, a gold necklace and a mule chariot. Sir, teach me the deity you worship.'
chandogya-4-2-2.meaning: The king offers the gifts and asks to be taught.
chandogya-4-2-2.explanation: He asks for the secret of Raikva's wisdom.

chandogya-4-2-3.translation: The other replied, 'Keep them, Shudra, along with your cows!' Then Janashruti came again with a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a mule chariot and his daughter.
chandogya-4-2-3.meaning: Raikva turns him away, and the king returns with even more.
chandogya-4-2-3.explanation: Raikva calls the king 'Shudra', probably as a pun on his grief (shuc) rather than his caste. The king persists.

chandogya-4-2-4.translation: He said, 'Raikva, here are a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a mule chariot, this wife, and this village where you live. Sir, please teach me.'
chandogya-4-2-4.meaning: The king offers everything, even a village, and asks again.
chandogya-4-2-4.explanation: The king's sincerity is now clear.

chandogya-4-2-5.translation: Raising her face, Raikva said, 'You have brought these, Shudra; with this face alone you would have got me to speak.' The villages where he lived among the Mahavrishas are called Raikvaparna. He taught him:
chandogya-4-2-5.meaning: Raikva agrees to teach the king.
chandogya-4-2-5.explanation: Raikva accepts, and the place is named after him. His teaching follows.

chandogya-4-3-1.translation: Wind is the absorber. When fire goes out, it goes into the wind. When the sun sets, it goes into the wind. When the moon sets, it goes into the wind.
chandogya-4-3-1.meaning: Everything in nature finally dissolves into the wind.
chandogya-4-3-1.explanation: Raikva's teaching: the 'absorber' (samvarga) is what takes everything into itself.

chandogya-4-3-2.translation: When water dries up, it goes into the wind. For the wind absorbs all these. So much about the gods.
chandogya-4-3-2.meaning: Even water vanishes into the air.
chandogya-4-3-2.explanation: The outer absorber is the wind.

chandogya-4-3-3.translation: Now about the self. Breath is the absorber. When a person sleeps, speech goes into breath, as do the eye, the ear and the mind. For breath absorbs all these.
chandogya-4-3-3.meaning: In sleep, all our senses go into the breath.
chandogya-4-3-3.explanation: The inner absorber is breath, which keeps going when the senses rest.

chandogya-4-3-4.translation: These are the two absorbers: wind among the gods, breath among the senses.
chandogya-4-3-4.meaning: Wind outside and breath inside take everything back into themselves.

chandogya-4-3-5.translation: Once, while Shaunaka Kapeya and Abhipratarin Kakshaseni were being served food, a student begged from them. They gave him nothing.
chandogya-4-3-5.meaning: Two wealthy men refuse food to a hungry student.
chandogya-4-3-5.explanation: A short story illustrating the teaching.

chandogya-4-3-6.translation: He said: 'One god has swallowed four great ones; who is he, guardian of the world? Mortals do not see him, Kapeya, though he dwells in many forms, Abhipratarin. The one to whom this food belongs has not been given it.'
chandogya-4-3-6.meaning: The student says the food they refused really belongs to the all-absorbing god.
chandogya-4-3-6.explanation: The 'one god' is the absorber, Prajapati or breath; the food belongs to him and so to all.

chandogya-4-3-7.translation: Shaunaka Kapeya thought it over and replied: 'He is the self of the gods, the father of creatures, with golden teeth, the eater, the wise one. They say his greatness is great, for he eats what is not food without being eaten. That, student, is what we worship. Give him food.'
chandogya-4-3-7.meaning: The host recognises the student's wisdom and orders food for him.
chandogya-4-3-7.explanation: The host understands the riddle and honours the student.

chandogya-4-3-8.translation: So they gave to him. These five and those five make ten, which is the winning throw. So in all directions ten is food. This is Viraj, the eater of food. By it all this is seen. Whoever knows this sees all this and enjoys food.
chandogya-4-3-8.meaning: The two sets of five together make the perfect ten that feeds all.
chandogya-4-3-8.explanation: Wind, fire, sun, moon, water and breath, speech, eye, ear, mind make ten, matching the winning dice throw and the ten-syllable Viraj metre.

chandogya-4-4-1.translation: Satyakama Jabala said to his mother Jabala, 'Mother, I want to live as a student. What is my family line?'
chandogya-4-4-1.meaning: A boy wants to become a student and asks his mother about his family.
chandogya-4-4-1.explanation: The famous story of Satyakama, the honest boy, begins. A student had to state his gotra (lineage).

chandogya-4-4-2.translation: She said, 'I do not know your line, my son. I had you in my youth when I moved about a great deal as a servant. I do not know. But my name is Jabala and yours is Satyakama. So call yourself Satyakama Jabala.'
chandogya-4-4-2.meaning: His mother honestly tells him she does not know his father.
chandogya-4-4-2.explanation: The mother tells the plain truth, and gives him her own name.

chandogya-4-4-3.translation: He went to Haridrumata Gautama and said, 'Sir, I wish to live with you as a student. May I come to you?'
chandogya-4-4-3.meaning: The boy goes to a teacher and asks to study.

chandogya-4-4-4.translation: Gautama asked, 'What is your family line, dear boy?' He replied, 'I do not know, sir. I asked my mother, and she said, "I had you in my youth when I moved about a great deal as a servant. I do not know. My name is Jabala and yours is Satyakama." So I am Satyakama Jabala, sir.'
chandogya-4-4-4.meaning: The boy tells the teacher the whole truth.
chandogya-4-4-4.explanation: He repeats his mother's words exactly, hiding nothing.

chandogya-4-4-5.translation: Gautama said, 'Only a true brahmin would speak so. Bring firewood, dear boy; I will accept you, since you have not left the truth.' He took four hundred thin, weak cows and said, 'Look after these.' As he drove them off the boy said, 'I will not come back until they are a thousand.' He was away for years, until they became a thousand.
chandogya-4-4-5.meaning: The teacher accepts him for his honesty and sends him to tend cattle.
chandogya-4-4-5.explanation: Truthfulness, not birth, makes a true brahmin. The boy's patient service is also his training.

chandogya-4-5-1.translation: Then the bull said to him, 'Satyakama!' 'Sir,' he replied. 'We have become a thousand, dear boy. Take us to the teacher's house.'
chandogya-4-5-1.meaning: When the herd reaches a thousand, the bull speaks to him.
chandogya-4-5-1.explanation: In his solitude, nature itself begins to teach Satyakama.

chandogya-4-5-2.translation: 'Dear boy, let me teach you one quarter of Brahman.' 'Please teach me, sir.' The bull said: 'East is one part; west is one part; south is one part; north is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman called Shining.'
chandogya-4-5-2.meaning: One quarter of Brahman is made of east, west, south, north, and it is called 'Shining'.
chandogya-4-5-2.explanation: Each of Satyakama's four teachers from nature reveals one quarter of Brahman. The bull teaches the four directions.

chandogya-4-5-3.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as Shining becomes shining in this world and wins shining worlds.
chandogya-4-5-3.meaning: Meditating on this quarter makes one's life shining.
chandogya-4-5-3.explanation: Each quarter's name becomes the quality of the one who meditates on it.

chandogya-4-6-1.translation: 'The fire will teach you another quarter.' Next morning he drove the cows on. Where they stopped at evening, he lit a fire, penned the cows, laid on fuel and sat down west of the fire, facing east.
chandogya-4-6-1.meaning: Satyakama tends the cows and sits by the evening fire.
chandogya-4-6-1.explanation: The next teacher will be the fire itself.

chandogya-4-6-2.translation: The fire said to him, 'Satyakama!' 'Sir,' he replied.
chandogya-4-6-2.explanation: Nature continues to teach the patient student.

chandogya-4-6-3.translation: 'Dear boy, let me teach you one quarter of Brahman.' 'Please teach me, sir.' The fire said: 'Earth is one part; mid-air is one part; heaven is one part; the ocean is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman called Endless.'
chandogya-4-6-3.meaning: One quarter of Brahman is made of earth, mid-air, heaven, the ocean, and it is called 'Endless'.
chandogya-4-6-3.explanation: Each of Satyakama's four teachers from nature reveals one quarter of Brahman. The fire teaches the vast worlds.

chandogya-4-6-4.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as Endless becomes endless in this world and wins endless worlds.
chandogya-4-6-4.meaning: Meditating on this quarter makes one's life endless.
chandogya-4-6-4.explanation: Each quarter's name becomes the quality of the one who meditates on it.

chandogya-4-7-3.translation: 'Dear boy, let me teach you one quarter of Brahman.' 'Please teach me, sir.' The swan said: 'Fire is one part; the sun is one part; the moon is one part; lightning is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman called Luminous.'
chandogya-4-7-3.meaning: One quarter of Brahman is made of fire, the sun, the moon, lightning, and it is called 'Luminous'.
chandogya-4-7-3.explanation: Each of Satyakama's four teachers from nature reveals one quarter of Brahman. A swan teaches the lights of the world. (Verses 4.7.1–2, where the swan appears, are missing in the digital source.)

chandogya-4-7-4.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as Luminous becomes luminous in this world and wins luminous worlds.
chandogya-4-7-4.meaning: Meditating on this quarter makes one's life luminous.
chandogya-4-7-4.explanation: Each quarter's name becomes the quality of the one who meditates on it.

chandogya-4-8-1.translation: 'A diver-bird will teach you another quarter.' Next morning he drove the cows on. Where they stopped at evening, he lit a fire, penned the cows, laid on fuel and sat down west of the fire, facing east.
chandogya-4-8-1.meaning: Again Satyakama sits by the evening fire.
chandogya-4-8-1.explanation: The last of his nature-teachers is a water bird.

chandogya-4-8-2.translation: The diver-bird flew down to him and said, 'Satyakama!' 'Sir,' he replied.
chandogya-4-8-2.meaning: A water bird flies down and calls him.

chandogya-4-8-3.translation: 'Dear boy, let me teach you one quarter of Brahman.' 'Please teach me, sir.' The bird said: 'Breath is one part; the eye is one part; the ear is one part; the mind is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman called Grounded.'
chandogya-4-8-3.meaning: One quarter of Brahman is made of breath, the eye, the ear, the mind, and it is called 'Grounded'.
chandogya-4-8-3.explanation: Each of Satyakama's four teachers from nature reveals one quarter of Brahman. The last quarter is found within the person.

chandogya-4-8-4.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as Grounded becomes grounded, with a firm home, in this world and wins grounded, with a firm home, worlds.
chandogya-4-8-4.meaning: Meditating on this quarter makes one's life grounded, with a firm home,.
chandogya-4-8-4.explanation: Each quarter's name becomes the quality of the one who meditates on it.

chandogya-4-9-1.translation: He reached the teacher's house. The teacher said to him, 'Satyakama!' 'Sir,' he replied.
chandogya-4-9-1.explanation: After years away, he comes home with the herd.

chandogya-4-9-2.translation: 'Dear boy, you shine like one who knows Brahman. Who has taught you?' 'Beings other than men,' he said. 'But I would like you, sir, to teach me,'
chandogya-4-9-2.meaning: His teacher sees he has gained wisdom; Satyakama still asks to be taught by him.
chandogya-4-9-2.explanation: Even after learning from nature, he values a human teacher.

chandogya-4-9-3.translation: 'for I have heard from people like you that knowledge learned from a teacher is best.' So the teacher taught him the very same thing, and nothing was left out.
chandogya-4-9-3.meaning: The teacher confirms everything; nothing was missing.
chandogya-4-9-3.explanation: The story stresses the value of a teacher, yet also that sincere seekers can learn from all of life.

chandogya-4-10-1.translation: Upakosala Kamalayana lived as a student with Satyakama Jabala. He tended his fires for twelve years. Satyakama let his other students go home, but not him.
chandogya-4-10-1.meaning: A student serves his teacher for twelve years but is not allowed to graduate.
chandogya-4-10-1.explanation: Satyakama is now a teacher himself. A new story begins.

chandogya-4-10-2.translation: His wife said, 'The student has worked hard and tended the fires well. Don't let the fires blame you; teach him.' But he went away on a journey without teaching him.
chandogya-4-10-2.meaning: The teacher's wife pleads for the student, but the teacher leaves without teaching him.
chandogya-4-10-2.explanation: The teacher seems harsh, but he may be testing the student.

chandogya-4-10-3.translation: Out of grief the student stopped eating. The teacher's wife said, 'Student, eat. Why aren't you eating?' He said, 'This person has many desires going many ways. I am full of sorrows. I will not eat.'
chandogya-4-10-3.meaning: The student is so sad that he stops eating.
chandogya-4-10-3.explanation: His fast shows his deep longing for knowledge.

chandogya-4-10-4.translation: Then the fires said to one another, 'The student has worked hard and tended us well. Let us teach him.' They said to him, 'Breath is Brahman. Ka is Brahman. Kha is Brahman.'
chandogya-4-10-4.meaning: The sacred fires teach him: breath, joy and space are Brahman.
chandogya-4-10-4.explanation: Ka means joy and kha means space.

chandogya-4-10-5.translation: He said, 'I understand that breath is Brahman. But I do not understand joy and space.' They said, 'Joy is the same as space; space is the same as joy.' And they explained to him both breath and the space within it.
chandogya-4-10-5.meaning: Joy and space are one: true joy is boundless.
chandogya-4-10-5.explanation: Joy without limits, and limitless space that is joyful, together point to Brahman.

chandogya-4-11-1.translation: Then the household fire taught him: 'Earth, fire, food and sun. The person seen in the sun am I; I am he.'
chandogya-4-11-1.meaning: The household fire reveals that the being in the sun is itself.
chandogya-4-11-1.explanation: Each of the three sacred fires teaches Upakosala a meditation linking the fire with parts of the world.

chandogya-4-11-2.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on it destroys his wrong deeds, gains a world, lives his full span, lives long; his descendants do not die out. We serve him in this world and the next, whoever knows this and meditates on it.
chandogya-4-11-2.meaning: Meditating this way frees one from wrongdoing and brings a long, full life.
chandogya-4-11-2.explanation: The fires promise to serve the one who knows them, here and after death.

chandogya-4-12-1.translation: Then the southern fire taught him: 'Water, the directions, the stars and the moon. The person seen in the moon am I; I am he.'
chandogya-4-12-1.meaning: The southern fire reveals that the being in the moon is itself.
chandogya-4-12-1.explanation: Each of the three sacred fires teaches Upakosala a meditation linking the fire with parts of the world.

chandogya-4-12-2.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on it destroys his wrong deeds, gains a world, lives his full span, lives long; his descendants do not die out. We serve him in this world and the next, whoever knows this and meditates on it.
chandogya-4-12-2.meaning: Meditating this way frees one from wrongdoing and brings a long, full life.
chandogya-4-12-2.explanation: The fires promise to serve the one who knows them, here and after death.

chandogya-4-13-1.translation: Then the offering fire taught him: 'Breath, space, heaven and lightning. The person seen in the lightning am I; I am he.'
chandogya-4-13-1.meaning: The offering fire reveals that the being in the lightning is itself.
chandogya-4-13-1.explanation: Each of the three sacred fires teaches Upakosala a meditation linking the fire with parts of the world.

chandogya-4-13-2.translation: Whoever knows this and meditates on it destroys his wrong deeds, gains a world, lives his full span, lives long; his descendants do not die out. We serve him in this world and the next, whoever knows this and meditates on it.
chandogya-4-13-2.meaning: Meditating this way frees one from wrongdoing and brings a long, full life.
chandogya-4-13-2.explanation: The fires promise to serve the one who knows them, here and after death.

chandogya-4-14-1.translation: They said, 'Upakosala, dear boy, you now have our knowledge and the knowledge of the Self. But your teacher will tell you the way.' His teacher came back and called, 'Upakosala!'
chandogya-4-14-1.meaning: The fires say his teacher will show him the path; the teacher returns.
chandogya-4-14-1.explanation: The fires give knowledge, but the final step comes from the teacher.

chandogya-4-14-2.translation: 'Sir,' he replied. 'Your face shines like one who knows Brahman, dear boy. Who has taught you?' 'Who would teach me, sir?' he said, as if hiding it. Pointing to the fires he said, 'They look like this now, but they were different.' 'What did they tell you, dear boy?'
chandogya-4-14-2.meaning: The teacher sees the student has learned something and asks what.
chandogya-4-14-2.explanation: The student hints shyly that the fires taught him.

chandogya-4-14-3.translation: 'This,' he said. 'They told you only about the worlds, dear boy. I will tell you that: as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so wrong deeds do not cling to one who knows this.' 'Please tell me, sir.' He told him:
chandogya-4-14-3.meaning: The teacher promises a teaching that makes one untouched by wrongdoing, like a lotus leaf by water.
chandogya-4-14-3.explanation: The lotus leaf, which water rolls off, is a famous image of living in the world untouched by it.

chandogya-4-15-1.translation: 'The person seen in the eye is the Self,' he said. 'It is immortal and fearless; it is Brahman. Even if one pours butter or water into the eye, it runs off to the edges.'
chandogya-4-15-1.meaning: The Self seen in the eye is deathless and fearless; it is Brahman.
chandogya-4-15-1.explanation: Like the lotus leaf, the eye is untouched by what is poured into it.

chandogya-4-15-2.translation: They call it Samyadvama, for all good things come to it. All good things come to one who knows this.
chandogya-4-15-2.meaning: It is called the gatherer of all good things.
chandogya-4-15-2.explanation: Samyadvama means 'where all good things meet'.

chandogya-4-15-3.translation: It is also Vamani, for it leads all good things. One who knows this leads all good things.
chandogya-4-15-3.meaning: It is also called the bringer of good.

chandogya-4-15-4.translation: It is also Bhamani, for it shines in all worlds. One who knows this shines in all worlds.
chandogya-4-15-4.meaning: It is also called the shining one.

chandogya-4-15-5.translation: Whether or not people perform funeral rites for such a one, he goes into the flame; from the flame to the day, from the day to the bright half of the month, from that to the six months when the sun moves north, from those months to the year, from the year to the sun, from the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning. There a person who is not human leads him to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman. Those who go by it do not return to this human cycle.
chandogya-4-15-5.meaning: The knower goes by the path of light to Brahman and does not return to rebirth.
chandogya-4-15-5.explanation: This describes the 'path of the gods' (devayana), the bright road after death that leads beyond rebirth. The Gita (8.24) describes the same path.

chandogya-4-16-1.translation: The wind that blows is the sacrifice. As it moves it purifies all this; since it purifies all this as it moves, it is the sacrifice. Mind and speech are its two paths.
chandogya-4-16-1.meaning: The wind is like the sacrifice; it purifies everything. Mind and speech are its two tracks.
chandogya-4-16-1.explanation: The sacrifice moves along two tracks, the silent mind and the spoken word.

chandogya-4-16-2.translation: The Brahman priest shapes one of them with his mind; the hotri, adhvaryu and udgatri shape the other with speech. If, after the morning recitation has begun and before the closing verse, the Brahman priest speaks,
chandogya-4-16-2.meaning: The overseeing priest works with his mind, the others with their voices.
chandogya-4-16-2.explanation: The Brahman priest watches silently; speaking breaks his part.

chandogya-4-16-3.translation: he shapes only one track, and the other is lost. As a man walking on one leg or a chariot running on one wheel comes to harm, so the sacrifice comes to harm, and the patron with it. He is worse off for having sacrificed.
chandogya-4-16-3.meaning: A rite with only one track breaks down, like a one-wheeled chariot.
chandogya-4-16-3.explanation: The silent mind is as important as the spoken word.

chandogya-4-16-4.translation: But if, after the morning recitation has begun, the Brahman priest does not speak before the closing verse, they shape both tracks, and neither is lost.
chandogya-4-16-4.meaning: When the overseer keeps silent, both tracks stay whole.
chandogya-4-16-4.explanation: Silence and speech together make a complete rite.

chandogya-4-16-5.translation: As a man walking on two legs or a chariot running on two wheels stands firm, so the sacrifice stands firm, and the patron with it. He is better off for having sacrificed.
chandogya-4-16-5.meaning: With both tracks, the rite and the patron stand firm.

chandogya-4-17-1.translation: Prajapati brooded over the worlds and drew out their essences: fire from the earth, wind from the mid-air, the sun from heaven.
chandogya-4-17-1.meaning: The creator drew fire, wind and sun out of the three worlds.
chandogya-4-17-1.explanation: A creation passage explaining the source of the sacred words.

chandogya-4-17-2.translation: He brooded over these three gods and drew out their essences: the Rik verses from fire, the Yajus formulas from wind, the Saman chants from the sun.
chandogya-4-17-2.meaning: From fire, wind and sun came the three Vedas.
chandogya-4-17-2.explanation: Each Veda comes from one of the gods.

chandogya-4-17-3.translation: He brooded over the threefold knowledge and drew out its essences: bhuh from the Riks, bhuvah from the Yajus, svah from the Samans.
chandogya-4-17-3.meaning: From the Vedas came the three sacred words.
chandogya-4-17-3.explanation: The words bhuh, bhuvah, svah hold the essence of all the Vedas.

chandogya-4-17-4.translation: If the sacrifice is harmed in the Rik part, one should offer in the household fire saying 'bhuh svaha'. So by the essence and power of the Rik verses one mends the harm to the sacrifice.
chandogya-4-17-4.meaning: A mistake in the Rik part is mended with the word 'bhuh'.
chandogya-4-17-4.explanation: Each of the three sacred words fixes errors in one part of the rite.

chandogya-4-17-5.translation: If the sacrifice is harmed in the Yajus part, one should offer in the southern fire saying 'bhuvah svaha'. So by the essence and power of the Yajus verses one mends the harm to the sacrifice.
chandogya-4-17-5.meaning: A mistake in the Yajus part is mended with the word 'bhuvah'.
chandogya-4-17-5.explanation: Each of the three sacred words fixes errors in one part of the rite.

chandogya-4-17-6.translation: If the sacrifice is harmed in the Saman part, one should offer in the offering fire saying 'svah svaha'. So by the essence and power of the Saman verses one mends the harm to the sacrifice.
chandogya-4-17-6.meaning: A mistake in the Saman part is mended with the word 'svah'.
chandogya-4-17-6.explanation: Each of the three sacred words fixes errors in one part of the rite.

chandogya-4-17-7.translation: As one joins gold with borax, silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and wood with leather,
chandogya-4-17-7.meaning: Just as each metal is joined with the right binder,
chandogya-4-17-7.explanation: A craftsman's image: every material has its proper joining agent.

chandogya-4-17-8.translation: so one mends a harm to the sacrifice by the power of these worlds, these gods and this threefold knowledge. A sacrifice with such a knowing Brahman priest is well healed.
chandogya-4-17-8.meaning: so the right knowledge mends any flaw in a sacrifice.
chandogya-4-17-8.explanation: A knowing priest is like a healer for the ritual.

chandogya-4-17-9.translation: A sacrifice with such a knowing Brahman priest slopes to the north. There is a verse about such a priest: 'Wherever it turns, there he goes.'
chandogya-4-17-9.meaning: A wise overseer keeps the rite on course wherever it turns.

chandogya-4-17-10.translation: 'The Brahman priest alone protects the Kurus like a mare.' A Brahman priest who knows this protects the sacrifice, the patron and all the priests. So one should choose a Brahman priest who knows this, not one who does not.
chandogya-4-17-10.meaning: A knowing overseer protects everyone in the rite, so choose one who knows.
chandogya-4-17-10.explanation: Chapter 4 ends by stressing knowledge over mere function. (The digital source repeats this verse twice.)

chandogya-5-1-1.translation: Whoever knows the eldest and best becomes the eldest and best. Breath is the eldest and best.
chandogya-5-1-1.meaning: Breath is the first and greatest of our powers.
chandogya-5-1-1.explanation: Chapter 5 opens with the famous contest of the senses.

chandogya-5-1-2.translation: Whoever knows the richest becomes the richest among his people. Speech is the richest.
chandogya-5-1-2.meaning: Speech is the richest of our powers.
chandogya-5-1-2.explanation: Each sense has its own excellence.

chandogya-5-1-3.translation: Whoever knows the firm footing stands firm in this world and the next. The eye is the firm footing.
chandogya-5-1-3.explanation: We find our way with our eyes.

chandogya-5-1-4.translation: Whoever knows success has his wishes, divine and human, fulfilled. The ear is success.
chandogya-5-1-4.explanation: Through hearing we learn what we need.

chandogya-5-1-5.translation: Whoever knows the home becomes a home for his people. The mind is the home.
chandogya-5-1-5.meaning: The mind is the home of our powers.
chandogya-5-1-5.explanation: All the senses report to the mind.

chandogya-5-1-6.translation: Then the senses argued over who was the best, each saying, 'I am the best! I am the best!'
chandogya-5-1-6.meaning: The senses quarrelled over which of them was the greatest.

chandogya-5-1-7.translation: The senses went to their father Prajapati and said, 'Sir, which of us is the best?' He told them, 'The one whose leaving makes the body seem worst off is the best among you.'
chandogya-5-1-7.meaning: The creator says the best is the one whose absence hurts the body most.

chandogya-5-1-8.translation: Speech left. After a year away it came back and asked, 'How were you able to live without me?' 'Like the dumb who do not speak, breathing with breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind.' Then speech went back in.
chandogya-5-1-8.meaning: When speech left, the body went on living, like the dumb who do not speak.
chandogya-5-1-8.explanation: Each sense leaves for a year to prove its importance, but the body survives without it.

chandogya-5-1-9.translation: The eye left. After a year away it came back and asked, 'How were you able to live without me?' 'Like the blind who do not see, breathing with breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind.' Then the eye went back in.
chandogya-5-1-9.meaning: When the eye left, the body went on living, like the blind who do not see.
chandogya-5-1-9.explanation: Each sense leaves for a year to prove its importance, but the body survives without it.

chandogya-5-1-10.translation: The ear left. After a year away it came back and asked, 'How were you able to live without me?' 'Like the deaf who do not hear, breathing with breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, thinking with the mind.' Then the ear went back in.
chandogya-5-1-10.meaning: When the ear left, the body went on living, like the deaf who do not hear.
chandogya-5-1-10.explanation: Each sense leaves for a year to prove its importance, but the body survives without it.

chandogya-5-1-11.translation: The mind left. After a year away it came back and asked, 'How were you able to live without me?' 'Like small children without understanding, breathing with breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear.' Then the mind went back in.
chandogya-5-1-11.meaning: When the mind left, the body went on living, like small children without understanding.
chandogya-5-1-11.explanation: Each sense leaves for a year to prove its importance, but the body survives without it.

chandogya-5-1-12.translation: Then breath was about to leave. As a fine horse tears up the pegs it is tied to, it tore up the other senses. They all came to it and said, 'Sir, stay! You are the best of us. Do not leave.'
chandogya-5-1-12.meaning: When breath began to leave, all the others were torn loose and begged it to stay.
chandogya-5-1-12.explanation: The result is clear: without breath, nothing lives. Breath is the best.

chandogya-5-1-13.translation: Then speech said to it, 'The richness that I have is yours.' The eye said, 'The firm footing that I am is yours.'
chandogya-5-1-13.meaning: Speech and eye admit their gifts really belong to breath.
chandogya-5-1-13.explanation: Each sense hands its special quality over to breath.

chandogya-5-1-14.translation: The ear said, 'The success that I am is yours.' The mind said, 'The home that I am is yours.'
chandogya-5-1-14.meaning: Ear and mind also give their gifts to breath.
chandogya-5-1-14.explanation: All powers of a person rest in life itself.

chandogya-5-1-15.translation: So people do not call them 'speeches', 'eyes', 'ears' or 'minds'. They call them 'breaths', for breath is all of these.
chandogya-5-1-15.meaning: That is why all the senses are called 'breaths'.
chandogya-5-1-15.explanation: In Sanskrit the senses are called pranas, after the breath that keeps them alive.

chandogya-5-2-1.translation: Breath said, 'What will be my food?' They said, 'Whatever there is, even what dogs and birds eat.' So all this is the food of ana (breath); ana is its plain name. For one who knows this, nothing is not food.
chandogya-5-2-1.meaning: All that lives is food for breath.
chandogya-5-2-1.explanation: Ana is a name for breath; anna is food. For the knower, all things nourish.

chandogya-5-2-2.translation: Breath said, 'What will be my clothing?' They said, 'Water.' That is why people sip water before and after eating; they clothe breath. It gains clothing and is not naked.
chandogya-5-2-2.meaning: Water is breath's clothing, which is why we sip water before and after meals.
chandogya-5-2-2.explanation: An explanation of the custom of sipping water around meals (achamana).

chandogya-5-2-3.translation: Satyakama Jabala told this to Goshruti Vaiyaghrapadya and said, 'Even if one told this to a dry stump, branches would grow on it and leaves would sprout.'
chandogya-5-2-3.meaning: This teaching is so powerful it could bring a dead stump to life.
chandogya-5-2-3.explanation: Satyakama, met in chapter 4, now appears as a teacher of the breath doctrine.

chandogya-5-2-4.translation: If one wishes to attain greatness, one should be consecrated on the new-moon day, and on the full-moon night stir a mash of all herbs with curd and honey, offer ghee into the fire saying 'To the eldest and best, svaha!' and pour the remainder into the mash.
chandogya-5-2-4.meaning: A ritual for gaining greatness, using a mash of herbs, curd and honey.
chandogya-5-2-4.explanation: The breath teaching is turned into a rite. Each offering names one of the qualities from 5.1.

chandogya-5-2-5.translation: He should offer ghee saying 'To the richest, svaha!', 'To firm footing, svaha!', 'To success, svaha!', 'To the home, svaha!', each time pouring the remainder into the mash.
chandogya-5-2-5.meaning: Offerings are made to each of the senses' gifts.
chandogya-5-2-5.explanation: Richness, footing, success and home match speech, eye, ear and mind.

chandogya-5-2-6.translation: Then stepping back and holding the mash in his cupped hands, he murmurs: 'Your name is Ama, for all this is at home with you. You are the eldest and best, the king and ruler. May you lead me to eldest rank, to the best, to kingship and rule. May I be all this.'
chandogya-5-2-6.meaning: He prays to breath to give him greatness.
chandogya-5-2-6.explanation: Ama ('with') is a name for breath, which is present in everything.

chandogya-5-2-7.translation: Then he drinks a sip at each line of this verse: 'We choose that of Savitri', 'the food of the god', 'the best and all-sustaining', 'we meditate on the strength of Bhaga', and drinks it all. Cleaning the cup, he lies down behind the fire on a skin or bare ground, silent and still. If he sees a woman in a dream, he may know the rite has succeeded.
chandogya-5-2-7.meaning: He sips the mash with each line of a hymn to the sun, then sleeps and watches for a good dream.
chandogya-5-2-7.explanation: The verse is close to the Gayatri prayer to Savitri, the sun.

chandogya-5-2-8.translation: There is this verse: 'When during rites for a wish one sees a woman in a dream, one should know it brings success.'
chandogya-5-2-8.meaning: A dream of a woman means success.

chandogya-5-3-1.translation: Shvetaketu Aruneya came to the assembly of the Panchalas. Pravahana Jaivali asked him, 'Young man, has your father taught you?' 'Yes, sir.'
chandogya-5-3-1.meaning: A proud young scholar is questioned by a king.
chandogya-5-3-1.explanation: The famous teaching of the five fires begins. Shvetaketu is Uddalaka's son.

chandogya-5-3-2.translation: 'Do you know where people go from here when they die?' 'No, sir.' 'Do you know how they return?' 'No, sir.' 'Do you know where the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors part?' 'No, sir.'
chandogya-5-3-2.meaning: The king asks about life after death, and the young man cannot answer.
chandogya-5-3-2.explanation: The questions are about the destiny of the soul.

chandogya-5-3-3.translation: 'Do you know why that world is never filled up?' 'No, sir.' 'Do you know how at the fifth offering water comes to be called a person?' 'Not at all, sir.'
chandogya-5-3-3.meaning: He cannot answer the last two questions either.

chandogya-5-3-4.translation: 'Then why did you say you had been taught? How can someone who does not know these things call himself taught?' Distressed, he went to his father and said, 'Sir, you told me you had taught me without teaching me!'
chandogya-5-3-4.meaning: Embarrassed, the young man complains to his father.

chandogya-5-3-5.translation: 'That fellow of the warrior class asked me five questions, and I could not answer even one.' The father said, 'As you have told them to me, I do not know a single one. If I had known them, how could I not have told you?'
chandogya-5-3-5.meaning: The father admits he does not know the answers either.
chandogya-5-3-5.explanation: Uddalaka's honesty matches his son's frankness.

chandogya-5-3-6.translation: Gautama went to the king's place. The king honoured him on arrival. Next morning, in the assembly, the king said, 'Gautama, choose a gift of human wealth.' He said, 'Keep your human wealth, king. Tell me what you said to the boy.' The king was troubled.
chandogya-5-3-6.meaning: The father goes to the king, refuses wealth, and asks for the teaching.
chandogya-5-3-6.explanation: Gautama (Uddalaka) humbly seeks to learn from the king.

chandogya-5-3-7.translation: He told him to stay for a while, then said: 'As you have asked, Gautama: this knowledge has never before gone to brahmins. That is why rule in all the worlds has belonged to the warrior class.' Then he taught him:
chandogya-5-3-7.meaning: The king says this knowledge was kept by warriors until now.
chandogya-5-3-7.explanation: A striking claim: the teaching of rebirth came from kings, not priests.

chandogya-5-4-1.translation: That world (heaven), Gautama, is a fire. The sun is its fuel, rays its smoke, day its flame, the moon its embers, the stars its sparks.
chandogya-5-4-1.meaning: That world (heaven) is pictured as a sacrificial fire.
chandogya-5-4-1.explanation: This is the 'five fires' teaching (panchagni vidya): life passes through five fires, each turning an offering into something new.

chandogya-5-4-2.translation: Into this fire the gods offer faith. From that offering King Soma (the moon) arises.
chandogya-5-4-2.meaning: Offering faith into this fire produces King Soma (the moon).
chandogya-5-4-2.explanation: Each stage feeds the next in a cycle of life.

chandogya-5-5-1.translation: The rain-god, Gautama, is a fire. Wind is its fuel, cloud its smoke, lightning its flame, the thunderbolt its embers, rumblings of thunder its sparks.
chandogya-5-5-1.meaning: The rain-god is pictured as a sacrificial fire.
chandogya-5-5-1.explanation: This is the 'five fires' teaching (panchagni vidya): life passes through five fires, each turning an offering into something new.

chandogya-5-5-2.translation: Into this fire the gods offer King Soma. From that offering rain arises.
chandogya-5-5-2.meaning: Offering King Soma into this fire produces rain.
chandogya-5-5-2.explanation: Each stage feeds the next in a cycle of life.

chandogya-5-6-1.translation: The earth, Gautama, is a fire. The year is its fuel, space its smoke, night its flame, the directions its embers, the in-between directions its sparks.
chandogya-5-6-1.meaning: The earth is pictured as a sacrificial fire.
chandogya-5-6-1.explanation: This is the 'five fires' teaching (panchagni vidya): life passes through five fires, each turning an offering into something new.

chandogya-5-6-2.translation: Into this fire the gods offer rain. From that offering food arises.
chandogya-5-6-2.meaning: Offering rain into this fire produces food.
chandogya-5-6-2.explanation: Each stage feeds the next in a cycle of life.

chandogya-5-7-1.translation: Man, Gautama, is a fire. Speech is its fuel, breath its smoke, the tongue its flame, the eye its embers, the ear its sparks.
chandogya-5-7-1.meaning: Man is pictured as a sacrificial fire.
chandogya-5-7-1.explanation: This is the 'five fires' teaching (panchagni vidya): life passes through five fires, each turning an offering into something new.

chandogya-5-7-2.translation: Into this fire the gods offer food. From that offering semen arises.
chandogya-5-7-2.meaning: Offering food into this fire produces semen.
chandogya-5-7-2.explanation: Each stage feeds the next in a cycle of life.

chandogya-5-8-1.translation: Woman, Gautama, is a fire. Her lap is its fuel, the invitation its smoke, the womb its flame, what is done inside its embers, the pleasures its sparks.
chandogya-5-8-1.meaning: Woman is pictured as a sacrificial fire.
chandogya-5-8-1.explanation: This is the 'five fires' teaching (panchagni vidya): life passes through five fires, each turning an offering into something new.

chandogya-5-8-2.translation: Into this fire the gods offer semen. From that offering the embryo arises.
chandogya-5-8-2.meaning: Offering semen into this fire produces the embryo.
chandogya-5-8-2.explanation: Each stage feeds the next in a cycle of life.

chandogya-5-9-1.translation: So at the fifth offering water comes to be called a person. Covered in the membrane, the embryo lies within for ten or nine months, or however long, and then is born.
chandogya-5-9-1.meaning: After five stages, the offering becomes a human being.
chandogya-5-9-1.explanation: This answers the king's fifth question: water (as rain, food, seed) becomes a person.

chandogya-5-9-2.translation: Once born, he lives as long as his life lasts. When he has died and his time has come, they carry him to the fire, from which he came and from which he arose.
chandogya-5-9-2.meaning: At death a person returns to the fire from which he came.
chandogya-5-9-2.explanation: Cremation completes the cycle: the body goes back into fire.

chandogya-5-10-1.translation: Those who know this, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, go into the flame; from the flame to the day, from the day to the bright half of the month, from that to the six months when the sun moves north,
chandogya-5-10-1.meaning: Those who know and live with faith go by the path of light.
chandogya-5-10-1.explanation: The path of the gods begins, as in 4.15.5.

chandogya-5-10-2.translation: from the months to the year, from the year to the sun, from the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning. There a person who is not human leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods.
chandogya-5-10-2.meaning: This path leads to Brahman, beyond return.
chandogya-5-10-2.explanation: This answers the king's question about the path of the gods.

chandogya-5-10-3.translation: But those who in the village worship with sacrifices, good works and gifts go into the smoke; from smoke to night, from night to the dark half of the month, from that to the six months when the sun moves south. They do not reach the year.
chandogya-5-10-3.meaning: Those who live by rituals and good works go by the path of smoke.
chandogya-5-10-3.explanation: This is the path of the ancestors (pitriyana), which leads to return.

chandogya-5-10-4.translation: From the months they go to the world of the ancestors, from there to space, from space to the moon. That is King Soma, the food of the gods; the gods eat it.
chandogya-5-10-4.meaning: They reach the moon and stay among the gods for a time.
chandogya-5-10-4.explanation: Their merit is enjoyed in the moon world.

chandogya-5-10-5.translation: Having stayed there until their merit is used up, they return by the same way: into space, from space into wind; having become wind they become smoke; having become smoke they become mist,
chandogya-5-10-5.meaning: When their merit runs out, they come back down.
chandogya-5-10-5.explanation: The return journey through the elements.

chandogya-5-10-6.translation: having become mist they become cloud; having become cloud they rain down. They are born here as rice and barley, herbs and trees, sesame and beans. From there escape is very hard, for only when someone eats the food and sheds the seed do they become again.
chandogya-5-10-6.meaning: They fall as rain, enter plants and must wait to be eaten to be born again.
chandogya-5-10-6.explanation: A vivid account of rebirth through the food chain.

chandogya-5-10-7.translation: Those whose conduct here has been pleasant will soon enter a pleasant womb: of a brahmin, a kshatriya or a vaishya. But those whose conduct has been foul will soon enter a foul womb: of a dog, a pig or an outcast.
chandogya-5-10-7.meaning: Good conduct leads to a good birth, bad conduct to a bad one.
chandogya-5-10-7.explanation: One of the earliest statements of karma and rebirth. The social ranking reflects the attitudes of its time.

chandogya-5-10-8.translation: Those on neither path become small creatures that keep coming back: 'Be born and die.' This is the third state. That is why that world is never filled. So one should shun it. There is this verse:
chandogya-5-10-8.meaning: Those on neither path are reborn endlessly as tiny creatures.
chandogya-5-10-8.explanation: This answers why the other world never fills up.

chandogya-5-10-9.translation: 'One who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who violates his teacher's bed, one who kills a brahmin: these four fall, and the fifth is one who keeps company with them.'
chandogya-5-10-9.meaning: The worst wrongs bring a person down, and so does keeping their company.
chandogya-5-10-9.explanation: These are the 'great sins' in Vedic law.

chandogya-5-10-10.translation: But whoever knows these five fires is not stained by wrong, even if he keeps company with such people. He becomes pure, clean, and wins a world of merit, whoever knows this.
chandogya-5-10-10.meaning: Knowing the five fires keeps a person pure.
chandogya-5-10-10.explanation: The teaching ends with the purifying power of knowledge.

chandogya-5-11-1.translation: Prachinashala Aupamanyava, Satyayajna Paulushi, Indradyumna Bhallaveya, Jana Sharkarakshya and Budila Ashvatarashvi, great householders and very learned, met and discussed: 'What is our Self? What is Brahman?'
chandogya-5-11-1.meaning: Five learned householders ask: what is the Self, and what is Brahman?
chandogya-5-11-1.explanation: The teaching on Vaishvanara, the universal Self, begins.

chandogya-5-11-2.translation: They agreed: 'Sirs, Uddalaka Aruni is now studying this universal Self, Vaishvanara. Let us go to him.' They went to him.
chandogya-5-11-2.meaning: They go to Uddalaka to learn.
chandogya-5-11-2.explanation: Vaishvanara means 'common to all people', the universal Self.

chandogya-5-11-3.translation: He thought: 'These great householders will question me, and I may not be able to answer everything. Let me send them to someone else.'
chandogya-5-11-3.meaning: Uddalaka, unsure of himself, decides to send them elsewhere.
chandogya-5-11-3.explanation: Humility again: he knows the limits of his knowledge.

chandogya-5-11-4.translation: He said to them, 'Sirs, Ashvapati Kaikeya is now studying this universal Self. Let us go to him.' They went to him.
chandogya-5-11-4.meaning: He leads them to King Ashvapati.
chandogya-5-11-4.explanation: Once again a king holds the deepest knowledge.

chandogya-5-11-5.translation: When they arrived, he had each of them honoured separately. Rising in the morning he said: 'In my kingdom there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard, no one without a sacred fire, no one ignorant, no adulterer, much less an adulteress. Sirs, I am about to hold a sacrifice. I will give each of you as much as I give each priest. Please stay.'
chandogya-5-11-5.meaning: The king describes his good kingdom and offers them rich fees.
chandogya-5-11-5.explanation: A famous picture of an ideal kingdom. The king assumes they want wealth.

chandogya-5-11-6.translation: They said, 'One should speak of the very thing one has come for. You are now studying this universal Self. Teach it to us.'
chandogya-5-11-6.meaning: They say they came for knowledge, not wealth.
chandogya-5-11-6.explanation: The guests politely redirect the king.

chandogya-5-11-7.translation: He said, 'I will answer you tomorrow.' Next morning they came to him carrying firewood, as students do. Without initiating them, he said to them:
chandogya-5-11-7.meaning: They come as students, and he begins to teach.
chandogya-5-11-7.explanation: Carrying fuel was the sign of a student seeking a teacher.

chandogya-5-12-1.translation: 'Aupamanyava, what do you meditate on as the Self?' 'Heaven, your majesty.' 'That is the universal Self called Sutejas, the bright one. So in your family Soma is seen pressed, pressed forth and pressed out.'
chandogya-5-12-1.meaning: The first man meditates on heaven, which is only one part of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-12-1.explanation: Each student has grasped only one part of the whole.

chandogya-5-12-2.translation: 'You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever meditates on this universal Self so eats food, sees what is dear, and has sacred radiance in his family. But that is only the head of the Self,' he said. 'Your head would have fallen off if you had not come to me.'
chandogya-5-12-2.meaning: Heaven is only the head of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-12-2.explanation: His partial view brings rewards, but is incomplete and even dangerous.

chandogya-5-13-1.translation: Then he asked Satyayajna Paulushi, 'What do you meditate on as the Self?' 'The sun, your majesty.' 'That is the universal Self called Vishvarupa, the many-formed. So in your family many kinds of things are seen:'
