chandogya-5-13-1.meaning: This man meditates on the sun, only one part of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-13-1.explanation: The king shows each student that his view is true but partial.

chandogya-5-13-2.translation: 'a mule chariot ready, a slave girl, a gold necklace. You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever meditates on this universal Self so eats food, sees what is dear, and has sacred radiance in his family. But that is only the eye of the Self,' he said. 'You would have gone blind if you had not come to me.'
chandogya-5-13-2.meaning: The sun is only the eye of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-13-2.explanation: Wealth comes from his meditation, but his view is still partial.

chandogya-5-14-1.translation: Then he asked Indradyumna Bhallaveya, 'What do you meditate on as the Self?' 'The wind, your majesty.' 'That is the universal Self called Prithagvartman, the one of many paths. So gifts come to you from many sides and lines of chariots follow you.'
chandogya-5-14-1.meaning: This man meditates on the wind, only one part of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-14-1.explanation: The king shows each student that his view is true but partial.

chandogya-5-14-2.translation: 'You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever meditates on this universal Self so eats food, sees what is dear, and has sacred radiance in his family. But that is only the breath of the Self,' he said. 'Your breath would have left you if you had not come to me.'
chandogya-5-14-2.meaning: This is only the breath of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-14-2.explanation: Holding a part as the whole is incomplete, and the king warns of its danger.

chandogya-5-15-1.translation: Then he asked Jana Sharkarakshya, 'What do you meditate on as the Self?' 'Space, your majesty.' 'That is the universal Self called Bahula, the abundant. So you are abundant in children and wealth.'
chandogya-5-15-1.meaning: This man meditates on space, only one part of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-15-1.explanation: The king shows each student that his view is true but partial.

chandogya-5-15-2.translation: 'You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever meditates on this universal Self so eats food, sees what is dear, and has sacred radiance in his family. But that is only the trunk of the Self,' he said. 'Your body would have fallen apart if you had not come to me.'
chandogya-5-15-2.meaning: This is only the trunk of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-15-2.explanation: Holding a part as the whole is incomplete, and the king warns of its danger.

chandogya-5-16-1.translation: Then he asked Budila Ashvatarashvi, 'What do you meditate on as the Self?' 'Water, your majesty.' 'That is the universal Self called Rayi, wealth. So you are wealthy and well-fed.'
chandogya-5-16-1.meaning: This man meditates on water, only one part of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-16-1.explanation: The king shows each student that his view is true but partial.

chandogya-5-16-2.translation: 'You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever meditates on this universal Self so eats food, sees what is dear, and has sacred radiance in his family. But that is only the bladder of the Self,' he said. 'Your bladder would have burst if you had not come to me.'
chandogya-5-16-2.meaning: This is only the bladder of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-16-2.explanation: Holding a part as the whole is incomplete, and the king warns of its danger.

chandogya-5-17-1.translation: Then he asked Uddalaka Aruni, 'What do you meditate on as the Self?' 'The earth, your majesty.' 'That is the universal Self called Pratishtha, the foundation. So you are well established with children and cattle.'
chandogya-5-17-1.meaning: This man meditates on the earth, only one part of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-17-1.explanation: The king shows each student that his view is true but partial.

chandogya-5-17-2.translation: 'You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever meditates on this universal Self so eats food, sees what is dear, and has sacred radiance in his family. But that is only the feet of the Self,' he said. 'Your feet would have withered if you had not come to me.'
chandogya-5-17-2.meaning: This is only the feet of the universal Self.
chandogya-5-17-2.explanation: Holding a part as the whole is incomplete, and the king warns of its danger.

chandogya-5-18-1.translation: He said to them: 'You eat food knowing this universal Self as if it were separate things. But whoever meditates on this universal Self as measured from heaven to earth and as one's own self eats food in all worlds, in all beings, in all selves.'
chandogya-5-18-1.meaning: Each of you knew a part; the one who knows the whole Self eats in all worlds.
chandogya-5-18-1.explanation: The key teaching: the universal Self is one, spanning heaven to earth, and it is one's own self.

chandogya-5-18-2.translation: Of this universal Self, heaven is the head, the sun the eye, wind the breath, space the trunk, water the bladder, earth the feet. The chest is the altar, the hair the sacred grass, the heart the household fire, the mind the southern fire, the mouth the offering fire.
chandogya-5-18-2.meaning: The universe is one body, and the human body is a sacred altar.
chandogya-5-18-2.explanation: The whole cosmos is pictured as one person, and the body as a place of offering.

chandogya-5-19-1.translation: The first offering he makes, he should make saying, 'To prana, svaha!' Then the in-breath is satisfied.
chandogya-5-19-1.meaning: The first mouthful of a meal is an offering to the in-breath.
chandogya-5-19-1.explanation: Eating is turned into an inner fire-offering (pranagnihotra) to the universal Self within.

chandogya-5-19-2.translation: When the in-breath is satisfied, the eye is satisfied; when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied; when the sun is satisfied, heaven is satisfied; when heaven is satisfied, whatever heaven and the sun rule over is satisfied. And after that, he himself is satisfied with children, cattle, food, brilliance and sacred radiance.
chandogya-5-19-2.meaning: Feeding the in-breath satisfies the whole world, and the eater too.
chandogya-5-19-2.explanation: Each mouthful nourishes the powers of nature linked to that breath.

chandogya-5-20-1.translation: The second offering he makes, he should make saying, 'To vyana, svaha!' Then the diffused breath is satisfied.
chandogya-5-20-1.meaning: The second mouthful of a meal is an offering to the diffused breath.
chandogya-5-20-1.explanation: Eating is turned into an inner fire-offering (pranagnihotra) to the universal Self within.

chandogya-5-20-2.translation: When the diffused breath is satisfied, the ear is satisfied; then the moon; then the directions; then whatever the directions and moon rule over. And after that, he himself is satisfied with children, cattle, food, brilliance and sacred radiance.
chandogya-5-20-2.meaning: Feeding the diffused breath satisfies the whole world, and the eater too.
chandogya-5-20-2.explanation: Each mouthful nourishes the powers of nature linked to that breath.

chandogya-5-21-1.translation: The third offering he makes, he should make saying, 'To apana, svaha!' Then the out-breath is satisfied.
chandogya-5-21-1.meaning: The third mouthful of a meal is an offering to the out-breath.
chandogya-5-21-1.explanation: Eating is turned into an inner fire-offering (pranagnihotra) to the universal Self within.

chandogya-5-21-2.translation: When the out-breath is satisfied, speech is satisfied; then fire; then the earth; then whatever earth and fire rule over. And after that, he himself is satisfied with children, cattle, food, brilliance and sacred radiance.
chandogya-5-21-2.meaning: Feeding the out-breath satisfies the whole world, and the eater too.
chandogya-5-21-2.explanation: Each mouthful nourishes the powers of nature linked to that breath.

chandogya-5-22-1.translation: The fourth offering he makes, he should make saying, 'To samana, svaha!' Then the balancing breath is satisfied.
chandogya-5-22-1.meaning: The fourth mouthful of a meal is an offering to the balancing breath.
chandogya-5-22-1.explanation: Eating is turned into an inner fire-offering (pranagnihotra) to the universal Self within.

chandogya-5-22-2.translation: When the balancing breath is satisfied, the mind is satisfied; then the rain-god; then lightning; then whatever lightning and the rain-god rule over. And after that, he himself is satisfied with children, cattle, food, brilliance and sacred radiance.
chandogya-5-22-2.meaning: Feeding the balancing breath satisfies the whole world, and the eater too.
chandogya-5-22-2.explanation: Each mouthful nourishes the powers of nature linked to that breath.

chandogya-5-23-1.translation: The fifth offering he makes, he should make saying, 'To udana, svaha!' Then the upward breath is satisfied.
chandogya-5-23-1.meaning: The fifth mouthful of a meal is an offering to the upward breath.
chandogya-5-23-1.explanation: Eating is turned into an inner fire-offering (pranagnihotra) to the universal Self within.

chandogya-5-23-2.translation: When the upward breath is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; then the wind; then space; then whatever wind and space rule over. And after that, he himself is satisfied with children, cattle, food, brilliance and sacred radiance.
chandogya-5-23-2.meaning: Feeding the upward breath satisfies the whole world, and the eater too.
chandogya-5-23-2.explanation: Each mouthful nourishes the powers of nature linked to that breath.

chandogya-5-24-1.translation: If someone performs the fire offering without knowing this, it is as if he pushed aside the live coals and poured the offering on ashes.
chandogya-5-24-1.meaning: A ritual done without understanding is like pouring offerings on dead ashes.

chandogya-5-24-2.translation: But if one performs the fire offering knowing this, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, in all selves.
chandogya-5-24-2.meaning: Done with understanding, a simple offering reaches every being.
chandogya-5-24-2.explanation: Even eating, done with this knowledge, becomes a universal offering.

chandogya-5-24-3.translation: As the fluff of a reed thrown into fire is burned up, so all the wrongs of one who knows this and performs the fire offering are burned up.
chandogya-5-24-3.meaning: The knower's wrongs burn away like reed fluff in fire.
chandogya-5-24-3.explanation: A vivid image of purification through knowledge.

chandogya-5-24-4.translation: So even if one who knows this gives his leftovers to an outcast, it is an offering to the universal Self within him. There is this verse:
chandogya-5-24-4.meaning: For the knower, even giving leftovers to the lowest person is an offering to the divine.
chandogya-5-24-4.explanation: The universal Self is in everyone, so all giving is sacred.

chandogya-5-24-5.translation: 'As hungry children here gather round their mother, so all beings gather round the fire offering.'
chandogya-5-24-5.meaning: All beings depend on this offering as children depend on their mother.
chandogya-5-24-5.explanation: Chapter 5 closes with a tender image.

chandogya-6-1-1.translation: There was Shvetaketu Aruneya. His father said to him, 'Shvetaketu, live as a student. No one in our family, dear boy, goes unlearned and is a brahmin only by birth.'
chandogya-6-1-1.meaning: A father sends his son to study, as all their family has done.
chandogya-6-1-1.explanation: Chapter 6, one of the most famous in the Upanishads, begins: Uddalaka teaching his son Shvetaketu.

chandogya-6-1-2.translation: He went at twelve, and at twenty-four, having studied all the Vedas, he returned conceited, proud of his learning and arrogant. His father said to him,
chandogya-6-1-2.meaning: After twelve years of study, the son came back proud and arrogant.
chandogya-6-1-2.explanation: Book learning has made him vain.

chandogya-6-1-3.translation: 'Shvetaketu, since you are so conceited, proud of your learning and arrogant, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known?' 'How can there be such a teaching, sir?'
chandogya-6-1-3.meaning: The father asks: did you learn the one thing that makes everything else known?
chandogya-6-1-3.explanation: The great question of the chapter: what is the one thing that, once known, makes all known?

chandogya-6-1-4.translation: 'Just as, dear boy, by knowing one lump of clay everything made of clay is known; the change is only a name, a word-handle; the truth is just clay;
chandogya-6-1-4.meaning: Know clay, and you know every pot; their differences are only names.
chandogya-6-1-4.explanation: A famous analogy: forms and names change, but the substance is one.

chandogya-6-1-5.translation: just as, by knowing one copper ornament everything made of copper is known; the change is only a name, a word-handle; the truth is just copper;
chandogya-6-1-5.meaning: Know copper, and you know everything made of copper.
chandogya-6-1-5.explanation: A second example of the same idea.

chandogya-6-1-6.translation: just as, by knowing one nail-cutter everything made of iron is known; the change is only a name, a word-handle; the truth is just iron; so, dear boy, is that teaching.'
chandogya-6-1-6.meaning: Know iron, and you know all iron tools. So it is with the deepest truth.
chandogya-6-1-6.explanation: The third example; the teaching will reveal the one reality behind all things.

chandogya-6-1-7.translation: 'Surely my respected teachers did not know this, for if they had, why would they not have told me? Please, sir, tell it to me.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-1-7.meaning: The humbled son asks his father to teach him.
chandogya-6-1-7.explanation: Shvetaketu's pride gives way to the wish to learn.

chandogya-6-2-1.translation: 'In the beginning, dear boy, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Some say that in the beginning this was non-being alone, one only, without a second, and from non-being, being was born.
chandogya-6-2-1.meaning: In the beginning there was only Being, one without a second.
chandogya-6-2-1.explanation: Ekam evadvitiyam, 'one only, without a second', is one of the most quoted phrases in Indian philosophy.

chandogya-6-2-2.translation: But how could that be, dear boy? How could being be born from non-being? No, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
chandogya-6-2-2.meaning: Something cannot come from nothing; Being was always there.
chandogya-6-2-2.explanation: Uddalaka rejects the idea that the world came from nothing.

chandogya-6-2-3.translation: It thought, "May I be many; may I grow." It sent forth heat. That heat thought, "May I be many; may I grow." It sent forth water. So whenever a person grieves or sweats, water comes from heat.
chandogya-6-2-3.meaning: Being wished to become many and created heat, and heat created water.
chandogya-6-2-3.explanation: Creation as Being's own wish to multiply. Tears and sweat are everyday proof that water comes from heat.

chandogya-6-3-1.translation: Of these beings there are only three origins: born from an egg, born alive, and born from a sprout.
chandogya-6-3-1.meaning: All living things come from eggs, wombs or seeds.
chandogya-6-3-1.explanation: A simple biology of the time.

chandogya-6-3-2.translation: That deity thought, "Let me enter these three deities with this living self and bring out names and forms."
chandogya-6-3-2.meaning: Being decided to enter the elements as the living self and give them names and forms.
chandogya-6-3-2.explanation: Being enters creation as the life (jiva) in all things.

chandogya-6-3-3.translation: "Let me make each of them threefold." So that deity entered these three deities with this living self and brought out names and forms.
chandogya-6-3-3.meaning: Being mixed each element with the other two.
chandogya-6-3-3.explanation: The 'threefolding' (trivritkarana) explains why all things contain all three elements.

chandogya-6-3-4.translation: It made each of them threefold. Now learn from me, dear boy, how each of these three deities becomes threefold.
chandogya-6-3-4.meaning: The father will now explain how each thing contains all three elements.
chandogya-6-3-4.explanation: Introduction to the examples that follow.

chandogya-6-4-1.translation: The red colour of fire is the colour of heat; the white is that of water; the black is that of food. So the 'fire-ness' of fire has gone. It is just a name, a word-handle, a change; the truth is only the three colours.
chandogya-6-4-1.meaning: Fire is really a mix of three elements; the rest is just a name.
chandogya-6-4-1.explanation: Everything is made of heat, water and food (earth), combined. Names describe changes, not the underlying reality.

chandogya-6-4-2.translation: The red colour of the sun is the colour of heat; the white is that of water; the black is that of food. So the 'the sun-ness' of the sun has gone. It is just a name, a word-handle, a change; the truth is only the three colours.
chandogya-6-4-2.meaning: The sun is really a mix of three elements; the rest is just a name.
chandogya-6-4-2.explanation: Everything is made of heat, water and food (earth), combined. Names describe changes, not the underlying reality.

chandogya-6-4-3.translation: The red colour of the moon is the colour of heat; the white is that of water; the black is that of food. So the 'the moon-ness' of the moon has gone. It is just a name, a word-handle, a change; the truth is only the three colours.
chandogya-6-4-3.meaning: The moon is really a mix of three elements; the rest is just a name.
chandogya-6-4-3.explanation: Everything is made of heat, water and food (earth), combined. Names describe changes, not the underlying reality.

chandogya-6-4-4.translation: The red colour of lightning is the colour of heat; the white is that of water; the black is that of food. So the 'lightning-ness' of lightning has gone. It is just a name, a word-handle, a change; the truth is only the three colours.
chandogya-6-4-4.meaning: Lightning is really a mix of three elements; the rest is just a name.
chandogya-6-4-4.explanation: Everything is made of heat, water and food (earth), combined. Names describe changes, not the underlying reality.

chandogya-6-4-5.translation: Knowing this, the great householders and scholars of old said, 'No one can now mention to us anything unheard, unthought or unknown.' For they knew it from these.
chandogya-6-4-5.meaning: Wise people of old said nothing could surprise them, because they knew this.
chandogya-6-4-5.explanation: Knowing the three elements, they understood everything made from them.

chandogya-6-4-6.translation: Whatever seemed red, they knew was the colour of heat; whatever seemed white, the colour of water; whatever seemed black, the colour of food.
chandogya-6-4-6.meaning: They saw the three elements in every colour.
chandogya-6-4-6.explanation: Everything visible is a mix of the three.

chandogya-6-4-7.translation: Whatever seemed unknown, they knew was a combination of these three deities. Now learn from me, dear boy, how these three deities, on reaching a person, each become threefold.
chandogya-6-4-7.meaning: Even what was unclear they understood as a mix of the three. Next: how they work in a person.
chandogya-6-4-7.explanation: The teaching moves from the world to the human body.

chandogya-6-5-1.translation: Food when eaten is divided three ways. Its coarsest part becomes waste, its middle part flesh, its finest part mind.
chandogya-6-5-1.meaning: The food we eat becomes waste, flesh and mind.
chandogya-6-5-1.explanation: The mind is pictured as the finest product of food.

chandogya-6-5-2.translation: Water when drunk is divided three ways. Its coarsest part becomes urine, its middle part blood, its finest part breath.
chandogya-6-5-2.meaning: Water becomes urine, blood and breath.
chandogya-6-5-2.explanation: Breath is the finest product of water.

chandogya-6-5-3.translation: Heat when eaten is divided three ways. Its coarsest part becomes bone, its middle part marrow, its finest part speech.
chandogya-6-5-3.meaning: Heat (in oils and fats) becomes bone, marrow and speech.
chandogya-6-5-3.explanation: Speech is the finest product of heat.

chandogya-6-5-4.translation: 'For the mind, dear boy, is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-5-4.meaning: Mind comes from food, breath from water, speech from heat.
chandogya-6-5-4.explanation: A materialist-sounding summary, which the father will soon go beyond.

chandogya-6-6-1.translation: 'When curd is churned, dear boy, its finest part rises up and becomes butter.
chandogya-6-6-1.meaning: Churned curd gives butter at the top.
chandogya-6-6-1.explanation: An everyday image to explain how the finest part rises.

chandogya-6-6-2.translation: In the same way, dear boy, when food is eaten its finest part rises up and becomes mind.
chandogya-6-6-2.meaning: So too, the finest part of food becomes mind.
chandogya-6-6-2.explanation: The mind is the 'butter' of food.

chandogya-6-6-3.translation: When water is drunk, dear boy, its finest part rises up and becomes breath.
chandogya-6-6-3.meaning: The finest part of water becomes breath.

chandogya-6-6-4.translation: When heat is eaten, dear boy, its finest part rises up and becomes speech.
chandogya-6-6-4.meaning: The finest part of heat (in oils) becomes speech.

chandogya-6-6-5.translation: 'For the mind, dear boy, is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-6-5.meaning: Mind, breath and speech come from food, water and heat.
chandogya-6-6-5.explanation: The father now proves this with an experiment.

chandogya-6-7-1.translation: 'A person, dear boy, has sixteen parts. Do not eat for fifteen days, but drink water as you like. Breath is made of water, so it will not be cut off if you drink.'
chandogya-6-7-1.meaning: The father asks his son to fast for fifteen days, drinking only water.
chandogya-6-7-1.explanation: An experiment to show that the mind depends on food.

chandogya-6-7-2.translation: He did not eat for fifteen days. Then he came to his father and said, 'What shall I recite, sir?' 'The Rik verses, the Yajus formulas, the Saman chants, dear boy.' He said, 'They do not come to me, sir.'
chandogya-6-7-2.meaning: After fasting, the son cannot remember the Vedas.

chandogya-6-7-3.translation: He said to him, 'Dear boy, just as of a great fire only one ember the size of a firefly may be left, which cannot burn much, so of your sixteen parts only one is left, and with it you cannot recall the Vedas. Eat, and then you will understand me.'
chandogya-6-7-3.meaning: Your mind is like a fire burned down to one tiny ember. Eat, and you will see.
chandogya-6-7-3.explanation: A clear image of a weakened mind.

chandogya-6-7-4.translation: He ate and came to him. Whatever he asked, he answered it all.

chandogya-6-7-5.translation: He said to him, 'Dear boy, just as when one ember the size of a firefly is left from a great fire, and one feeds it with straw and makes it blaze, it can burn much more,
chandogya-6-7-5.meaning: An ember fed with straw blazes up again.
chandogya-6-7-5.explanation: The image of the fire continues.

chandogya-6-7-6.translation: so of your sixteen parts one was left; fed with food, it blazed up, and with it you now recall the Vedas. For the mind, dear boy, is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat.' Then he understood it, he understood.
chandogya-6-7-6.meaning: Food rekindled his mind, as straw rekindles an ember.
chandogya-6-7-6.explanation: Shvetaketu learns by experience, not just by being told.

chandogya-6-8-1.translation: Uddalaka Aruni said to his son Shvetaketu, 'Learn from me the nature of sleep, dear boy. When a person sleeps, he has merged with Being; he has gone to his own. That is why they say he sleeps (svapiti), for he has gone to his own (svam apita).'
chandogya-6-8-1.meaning: In deep sleep we return to pure Being, our true home.
chandogya-6-8-1.explanation: Word-play on svapiti, 'sleeps', and svam apita, 'gone to one's own'.

chandogya-6-8-2.translation: As a bird tied by a string flies in every direction and, finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down at its tether, so the mind, dear boy, flies in every direction and, finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down in breath. For the mind, dear boy, is tethered to breath.
chandogya-6-8-2.meaning: The restless mind, like a tied bird, finally rests in breath.
chandogya-6-8-2.explanation: A beautiful image of the mind's wandering and its return home.

chandogya-6-8-3.translation: Learn from me hunger and thirst, dear boy. When a person is hungry, water carries away what he has eaten. As we speak of a cattle-leader, horse-leader or people-leader, so water is called 'food-leader' (ashanaya), hunger. Know that this body is a sprout that has sprung up; it cannot be without a root.
chandogya-6-8-3.meaning: Water digests our food, and our body is a sprout that must have a root.
chandogya-6-8-3.explanation: The body is like a shoot; the father will trace its roots.

chandogya-6-8-4.translation: Where could its root be except in food? In the same way, dear boy, with food as the sprout, seek water as the root; with water as the sprout, seek heat as the root; with heat as the sprout, seek Being as the root. All these creatures, dear boy, have Being as their root, Being as their home, Being as their support.
chandogya-6-8-4.meaning: Trace everything back and you find that all beings are rooted in Being.
chandogya-6-8-4.explanation: Body comes from food, food from water, water from heat, heat from Being.

chandogya-6-8-5.translation: When a person is thirsty, heat carries away what he has drunk. As we speak of a cattle-leader, horse-leader or people-leader, so heat is called 'water-leader' (udanya), thirst. Know that this body is a sprout that has sprung up; it cannot be without a root.
chandogya-6-8-5.meaning: Heat dries up the water we drink; again the body is a sprout.

chandogya-6-8-6.translation: Where could its root be except in water? With water as the sprout, seek heat as the root; with heat as the sprout, seek Being as the root. All these creatures have Being as their root, home and support. How the three deities each become threefold on reaching a person has been told. When a person dies, dear boy, his speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, and heat into the highest deity.
chandogya-6-8-6.meaning: At death, speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, and heat into Being.
chandogya-6-8-6.explanation: The process of dying traced in reverse to the source.

chandogya-6-8-7.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-8-7.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-8-7.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. This is the first of nine times the father repeats it.

chandogya-6-9-1.translation: 'As bees, dear boy, make honey by gathering the juices of many different trees and reducing them to one juice,
chandogya-6-9-1.meaning: Bees mix nectar from many flowers into one honey.
chandogya-6-9-1.explanation: The first of the father's famous illustrations of oneness.

chandogya-6-9-2.translation: and as those juices cannot tell "I am the juice of this tree" or "I am the juice of that tree", so all these creatures, dear boy, on merging into Being, do not know that they have merged into Being.
chandogya-6-9-2.meaning: In deep sleep or at death, beings merge into Being without knowing it, like nectars in honey.
chandogya-6-9-2.explanation: Individual identity disappears in the one source.

chandogya-6-9-3.translation: Whatever they are here, tiger or lion, wolf or boar, worm or moth, gnat or mosquito, that they become again.
chandogya-6-9-3.meaning: Then they return as whatever they were before.
chandogya-6-9-3.explanation: After sleep, each creature wakes up as itself.

chandogya-6-9-4.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-9-4.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-9-4.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. Here it follows the image of the honey.

chandogya-6-10-1.translation: 'These rivers, dear boy, flow east and west. From ocean they go to ocean and become the ocean itself. There they do not know "I am this river" or "I am that river".
chandogya-6-10-1.meaning: Rivers flow into the ocean and no longer know which river they were.
chandogya-6-10-1.explanation: The second illustration, one of the most loved in the Upanishads.

chandogya-6-10-2.translation: In the same way, dear boy, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know that they have come from Being. Whatever they are here, tiger or lion, wolf or boar, worm or moth, gnat or mosquito, that they become again.
chandogya-6-10-2.meaning: Beings come from Being without knowing it, and live as themselves.
chandogya-6-10-2.explanation: We all arise from the same source but forget it.

chandogya-6-10-3.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-10-3.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-10-3.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. Here it follows the image of the rivers and the ocean.

chandogya-6-11-1.translation: 'Dear boy, if someone strikes this great tree at its root, it would bleed sap but live; if at its middle, it would bleed but live; if at its top, it would bleed but live. Filled with the living self, it stands drinking in moisture and rejoicing.
chandogya-6-11-1.meaning: A tree lives on when struck, because life fills all of it.
chandogya-6-11-1.explanation: The third illustration: the life within a tree.

chandogya-6-11-2.translation: If life leaves one branch, that branch dries up; if it leaves a second, that dries up; if a third, that dries up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up.
chandogya-6-11-2.meaning: Where life departs, the tree withers.
chandogya-6-11-2.explanation: Life, not wood, is what makes the tree alive.

chandogya-6-11-3.translation: 'In the same way, dear boy, know this,' he said. 'This body dies when life has left it; life itself does not die. That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-11-3.meaning: The body dies, but the life within never dies; and that life is you.
chandogya-6-11-3.explanation: A key teaching on the deathless self.

chandogya-6-12-1.translation: 'Bring me a fig from there.' 'Here it is, sir.' 'Break it.' 'It is broken, sir.' 'What do you see?' 'These tiny seeds, sir.' 'Break one of them.' 'It is broken, sir.' 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all, sir.'
chandogya-6-12-1.meaning: Inside a fig seed, the son sees nothing.
chandogya-6-12-1.explanation: The fourth illustration: the banyan seed.

chandogya-6-12-2.translation: He said to him, 'Dear boy, from that finest essence which you do not see, this great banyan tree stands. Have faith, dear boy.'
chandogya-6-12-2.meaning: From the invisible essence in a tiny seed grows a huge tree. Have faith.
chandogya-6-12-2.explanation: What is too fine to see is the source of all that we see.

chandogya-6-12-3.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-12-3.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-12-3.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. Here it follows the image of the banyan seed.

chandogya-6-13-1.translation: 'Put this salt in water and come to me in the morning.' He did so. The father said, 'Bring me the salt you put in the water last night.' He felt for it but did not find it,
chandogya-6-13-1.meaning: Salt dissolved in water cannot be found.
chandogya-6-13-1.explanation: The fifth illustration: salt in water.

chandogya-6-13-2.translation: for it had dissolved. 'Sip from the top. How is it?' 'Salty.' 'Sip from the middle. How is it?' 'Salty.' 'Sip from the bottom. How is it?' 'Salty.' 'Throw it away and come to me.' He did so, but it was still there. The father said, 'You do not see Being here, dear boy, yet it is right here.'
chandogya-6-13-2.meaning: Unseen, the salt is in every drop; so Being is everywhere, though unseen.
chandogya-6-13-2.explanation: Being cannot be seen, but it can be tasted everywhere.

chandogya-6-13-3.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-13-3.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-13-3.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. Here it follows the image of the salt in water.

chandogya-6-14-1.translation: 'Dear boy, suppose someone brought a man from Gandhara with his eyes covered and left him in a lonely place. He would wander east, north, south or west, crying out, "I was brought here with my eyes covered and left here with my eyes covered!"
chandogya-6-14-1.meaning: Like a blindfolded man left far from home, we are lost.
chandogya-6-14-1.explanation: The sixth illustration: the lost traveller.

chandogya-6-14-2.translation: If someone took off his blindfold and told him, "Gandhara is that way; go that way," he would go from village to village, asking his way, and, being wise and sensible, would reach Gandhara. In the same way, a person who has a teacher knows. For him there is delay only until he is freed; then he arrives.
chandogya-6-14-2.meaning: A teacher removes the blindfold and points the way home.
chandogya-6-14-2.explanation: The role of the teacher in finding one's true self.

chandogya-6-14-3.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-14-3.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-14-3.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. Here it follows the image of the traveller from Gandhara.

chandogya-6-15-1.translation: 'Dear boy, when a person is gravely ill, his relatives gather round and ask, "Do you know me? Do you know me?" As long as his speech has not merged into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat and heat into the highest deity, he knows them.
chandogya-6-15-1.meaning: A dying person still recognises his family while his faculties remain.
chandogya-6-15-1.explanation: The seventh illustration: the process of dying.

chandogya-6-15-2.translation: But when his speech has merged into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat and heat into the highest deity, he no longer knows them.
chandogya-6-15-2.meaning: When everything has merged into Being, he no longer recognises anyone.
chandogya-6-15-2.explanation: At death, individual awareness returns to the source.

chandogya-6-15-3.translation: 'That finest essence is the Self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu.' 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said.
chandogya-6-15-3.meaning: The subtle essence in everything is the one Self, and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-15-3.explanation: 'Tat tvam asi', 'That you are', is one of the four great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads. Here it follows the image of the dying man.

chandogya-6-16-1.translation: 'Dear boy, they bring a man with his hands held, saying, "He has stolen! He has committed theft! Heat the axe for him!" If he did it, he makes himself false. Committed to falsehood and covering himself with falsehood, he takes hold of the heated axe; he is burned and then put to death.
chandogya-6-16-1.meaning: An accused thief who lies is burned by the hot axe and punished.
chandogya-6-16-1.explanation: An ancient trial by ordeal is used as the final illustration.

chandogya-6-16-2.translation: But if he did not do it, he makes himself true. Committed to truth and covering himself with truth, he takes hold of the heated axe; he is not burned, and he is set free.
chandogya-6-16-2.meaning: An innocent man who holds to truth is not burned and goes free.
chandogya-6-16-2.explanation: Truth protects; it is the Self's own nature.

chandogya-6-16-3.translation: As he is not burned there, so this whole world has that as its Self. That is the truth. That is the Self. That you are, Shvetaketu. And he understood it, he understood.
chandogya-6-16-3.meaning: As truth protects the innocent, the true Self is in all; and that Self is you.
chandogya-6-16-3.explanation: The ninth and last 'That you are'. Shvetaketu finally understands.

chandogya-7-1-1.translation: 'Teach me, sir,' said Narada, approaching Sanatkumara. He said to him, 'Come to me with what you know; then I will tell you what lies beyond it.' Narada said:
chandogya-7-1-1.meaning: Narada asks Sanatkumara to teach him.
chandogya-7-1-1.explanation: Chapter 7 begins: the sage Narada, learned in everything, comes to the wise Sanatkumara.

chandogya-7-1-2.translation: 'Sir, I know the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva as the fourth, epics and ancient lore as the fifth Veda, grammar, rites for ancestors, mathematics, omens, chronology, logic, ethics, etymology, the science of Vedic study, the science of spirits, the science of weapons, astronomy, and the arts of snake-charming and fine arts. This is what I know, sir.'
chandogya-7-1-2.meaning: Narada lists the many subjects he has mastered.
chandogya-7-1-2.explanation: An impressive list of the learning of the time.

chandogya-7-1-3.translation: 'But, sir, I know only words; I do not know the Self. I have heard from people like you that one who knows the Self crosses beyond sorrow. I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across sorrow.' He said to him, 'All that you have learned is only name.'
chandogya-7-1-3.meaning: For all his learning, Narada is sad, because he does not know the Self.
chandogya-7-1-3.explanation: A deeply human confession: knowledge without self-knowledge does not end sorrow.

chandogya-7-1-4.translation: 'The Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda, the Atharva, epics and lore, and all these sciences are only name. Meditate on name.'
chandogya-7-1-4.meaning: All his learning is only names; start by meditating on name.
chandogya-7-1-4.explanation: Sanatkumara begins a ladder of fifteen steps from name to the infinite.

chandogya-7-1-5.translation: Whoever meditates on name as Brahman can move freely as far as name reaches. 'Sir, is there anything greater than name?' 'There is something greater than name.' 'Then please tell me, sir.'
chandogya-7-1-5.meaning: Seeing name as Brahman gives freedom within its range, but there is something greater.
chandogya-7-1-5.explanation: Sanatkumara leads Narada step by step from lesser things to greater, toward the infinite.

chandogya-7-2-1.translation: Speech is greater than name. Speech makes known the Vedas and all the sciences; heaven and earth, wind and space, water and heat, gods and humans, animals and birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, insects and ants; right and wrong, truth and falsehood, good and bad, pleasant and unpleasant. If there were no speech, neither right nor wrong would be known, nor truth nor falsehood, nor good nor bad, nor pleasant nor unpleasant. Speech makes all this known. Meditate on speech.
chandogya-7-2-1.meaning: Speech is greater than names, for it makes everything known, even right and wrong.
chandogya-7-2-1.explanation: The second step on the ladder.

chandogya-7-2-2.translation: Whoever meditates on speech as Brahman can move freely as far as speech reaches. 'Sir, is there anything greater than speech?' 'There is something greater than speech.' 'Then please tell me, sir.'
chandogya-7-2-2.meaning: Seeing speech as Brahman gives freedom within its range, but there is something greater.
chandogya-7-2-2.explanation: Sanatkumara leads Narada step by step from lesser things to greater, toward the infinite.

chandogya-7-3-1.translation: Mind is greater than speech. As a closed fist holds two acorns, two berries or two dice, so mind holds speech and name. When one thinks in the mind, 'Let me learn the hymns,' one learns them; 'Let me do my work,' one does it; 'Let me wish for sons and cattle,' one wishes; 'Let me wish for this world and the next,' one wishes. Mind is the self; mind is the world; mind is Brahman. Meditate on mind.
chandogya-7-3-1.meaning: Mind is greater than speech, for every action begins with a thought.

chandogya-7-3-2.translation: Whoever meditates on mind as Brahman can move freely as far as mind reaches. 'Sir, is there anything greater than mind?' 'There is something greater than mind.' 'Then please tell me, sir.'
chandogya-7-3-2.meaning: Seeing mind as Brahman gives freedom within its range, but there is something greater.
chandogya-7-3-2.explanation: Sanatkumara leads Narada step by step from lesser things to greater, toward the infinite.

chandogya-7-4-1.translation: Will is greater than mind. When one wills, then one thinks; then one utters speech, and utters it in name. In name the hymns become one, and in the hymns the rites.
chandogya-7-4-1.meaning: Will comes before thought, speech and action.
chandogya-7-4-1.explanation: The fourth step: will or intention (sankalpa).

chandogya-7-4-2.translation: All these have will as their meeting point, will as their self, and rest on will. Heaven and earth were formed by will; wind and space were formed; water and heat were formed. Through their forming, rain is formed; through rain, food; through food, the life-breaths; through the breaths, the hymns; through the hymns, rites; through rites, the world; through the world, everything. Such is will. Meditate on will.
chandogya-7-4-2.meaning: The whole universe is shaped by will, step by step.
chandogya-7-4-2.explanation: A chain from cosmic will down to the world we live in.

chandogya-7-4-3.translation: Whoever meditates on will as Brahman wins worlds formed by will, firm himself in firm worlds, established in established worlds, unwavering in unwavering worlds. He can move freely as far as will reaches. 'Sir, is there anything greater than will?' 'There is something greater than will.' 'Then please tell me, sir.'
chandogya-7-4-3.meaning: Meditating on will brings firm, stable worlds, but there is still something greater.

chandogya-7-5-1.translation: Thought is greater than will. When one considers, then one wills, then one thinks, then one utters speech, and utters it in name. In name the hymns become one, and in the hymns the rites.
chandogya-7-5-1.explanation: The fifth step: chitta, attention or understanding.

chandogya-7-5-2.translation: All these have thought as their meeting point, their self and their support. So even if someone knows much but lacks understanding, people say, 'He is nobody. Whatever he knows, if he really knew, he would not be so thoughtless.' But if someone knows little but has understanding, people listen to him. For thought is their meeting point, their self, their support. Meditate on thought.
chandogya-7-5-2.meaning: Understanding matters more than how much one knows.
chandogya-7-5-2.explanation: A timeless observation about wisdom versus mere information.

chandogya-7-5-3.translation: Whoever meditates on thought as Brahman wins worlds of thought, firm himself in firm worlds, established in established worlds, unwavering in unwavering worlds. He can move freely as far as thought reaches. 'Sir, is there anything greater than thought?' 'There is something greater than thought.' 'Then please tell me, sir.'
chandogya-7-5-3.meaning: Meditating on thought brings steady worlds, but there is still more.
